demands of coir based furnishings and building materials from the  domestic as well as 
international market. To achieve this, more funds should be allocated by the Ministry of 
MSME to the Coir Board. 
(Para 102) 
32 

Action Taken 
 
As observed by the Hon’ble Committee, the products of coir industry can contribute 
immensely for maintaining ecological balance.    ‘Coir-wood’ deserves special consideration 
as it is a substitute for wood and saves rain forest which in turn keeps reversing global 
warming. The coir wood has immense market potential both in the domestic and internati onal 
market.  A total number of three units for production of ‘coir -wood’ have been sanctioned 
under SFURTI so far.   Out of this, one unit is ready for operation and two units are under 
various stages of establishment. The Board proposes to establish more units to manufacture 
coir-wood under SFURTI in the current phase. Coir Board made efforts through Ministry of 
MSME to declare coir products under mandatory procurement by government sector and 
declare coir products as agricultural products. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
Ecological balance is essential for sustenance of various forms of life and the Coir 
Board is doing an excellent job by giving a substitute for wood in the form of coir wood.  
The coir wood can be a very good substitute for wood, prov ided that the production of 
coir wood is encouraged and a favourable environment is created for its production.  
Coir wood has also a huge potential for overseas market, which can contribute 
significantly for the growth of national economy. In order to enc ourage the Coir 
Industry, the Committee recommends that more SFURTI clusters should be set up in 
the Coir Producing areas to provide gainful employment to the youth; latest technology 
should be adopted for creating innovative and durable coir products; and  adequate 
budgetary provisions should also be made for the development, promotion and 
marketing of coir products.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
46. During its study visit to Kolkata, Hyderabad and Mumbai during January 2020, the 
Committee was informed by t he MSME Associations that the subsidy limit under the CLCS -
TUS may be enhanced to 25% as provided under other Schemes under the Ministry to SC/ST 
entrepreneurs. Thus, in order to increase the participation of SC/ST/Women entrepreneurs 
under the CLCS -TU Scheme, the percentage of subsidy may be increased under the scheme. 
The Committee recommends that the subsidy amount should be raised to 25% for  
SC/ST/Women entrepreneurs as provided under the Special Credit Linked Subsidy Schemes to 
attract more SC/ST/Wome n entrepreneurs for making it a meaningful scheme for these 
categories. 
(Para 135) 
Action Taken 
 
Ministry of MSME is also implementing a scheme similar to Credit Linked Capital 
Subsidy scheme specifically for SC -ST Entrepreneurs.   This scheme is known as Special 
CLCSS Scheme and it is being implemented through NSIC. The subsidy component under 
this scheme is 25%. 
 
 
33 

Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
 An unprecedented situation is prevailing because of Covid -19 pandemic, which 
has adversely affected every aspect of human life.  Industries are shutting down, 
production has decreased, jobs are lost.  To meet this situation, Hon’ble Prime Minister 
has given a vision of making India ‘Atmanirbhar’ and this vision can be achiev ed by 
promoting entrepreneurship among the citizens , which is possible by giving them right 
opportunities in the form of favourable entrepreneurial environment so that they may 
be encouraged to set up their ventures by taking advantage of various schemes r un by 
Government.  The Committee recommends that suitable modifications be made in the 
various schemes run by Ministry so as to attract more and more potential entrepreneurs 
to make the nation ‘Atmanirbhar’.   
  
Recommendation/Observation 
 
47. The Committee observes that there is constant decline in the number of beneficiaries 
benefitted in the last three years i.e. year 2016 -17, 2017-18 and 2018-19 Work-shed Scheme 
for Khadi Artisans. Even in the year 2018-19, the figure is less than half of the figure that was 
in 2016-17. The Committee desires to know the reason behind this decline. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that necessary steps should be taken to construct sufficient number of 
Workshed for improving the working conditions of Khadi Artisans of t he BPL Group. 
Moreover, the disbursements for the construction of Work -sheds should be made in a very 
transparent and time-bound manner. 
(Para 139) 
 
Action Taken 
 
KVIC is sanctioning funds for construction of Individual Worksheds and Group 
Worksheds to the Khadi Artisans every year, on the basis of funds sanctioned by the Ministry 
and the demand received from the KIs through respective State/Divisional Offices. 
  
An evaluation study on the implementation of Workshed Scheme has been conducted 
and the study report reveals that amount for construction of workshed is low in comparison to 
other prevailing schemes. Various State Governments are also providing housing benefits 
under their schemes. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
Workshed scheme was introduced for providing better work ing conditions to 
Khadi artisans and it seems that now the scheme has lost its purpose because of various 
other schemes run by the State Governments. The Committee , therefore, recommends 
that suitable modifications be made to make the Workshed Scheme more attractive vis a 
vis other schemes run by State Governments  and more benefits may be added to the 
scheme to make it popular among the artisans. The financial benefits provided under the 
construction of Workshed may be enhanced for  making the scheme more beneficial and 
attractive.  
 
34 

Recommendation/Observation 
 
48. In a visit of the Committee to Kolkata, Hyderabad and Mumbai in January, 2020, it 
came to the notice that although the CPSEs have made payments to the MSEs but still the 
portal showed pendency against the concerned CPSEs due to lack of updation of information 
on the Portal. The Committee recommends that a proper monitoring mechanism should be put 
in place to check such type of information on the SAMADHAAN portal and da ta about the 
payments made should be regularly updated and errors must be rectified immediately. 
 
(Para 143) 
Action Taken 
 
The updation of portal is being taken up by the respective MSEFCs. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
The Committee does not feel satisfied with the reply given by the Ministry.  The 
Committee re-iterates its recommendation that a proper monitoring mechanism be put 
in place to monitor and update the data in the Samadhaan Portal.  This would facilitate 
in mitigating avoidable stress a nd embarrassment to those CPSEs who have cleared 
their pending dues to the MSEs, besides giving a crystal clear picture of the information 
contained in the portal, which was the aim for creating it. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
49. The Committee is very co ncerned about this underutilization of budget repeatedly. 
Also, the BE of Rs. 30.00 crore seems significantly reduced against BE of Rs. 232.00 crore in 
year 2018 -19. To consider ASPIRE, an important and crucial scheme, for innovative 
entrepreneurship in ag ro-industry, the Committee is, however disappointed to note that only 
an amount of Rs. 30 crore has been proposed for 2020 -21. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that more budgetary provisions should be made for such an important scheme. 
Apart from this steps may be taken to restructure the Scheme to make it more attractive for 
potential entrepreneurs with proper assessment and planning to implement the scheme 
successfully and meaningfully. 
(Para 148) 
Action Taken 
 
 As suggested steps to restructure the s cheme shall be initiated based on the third party 
evaluation of the scheme which is to be undertaken during the current year. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
35 
 

Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
ASPIRE is one of the major and important Schemes of the Ministry, which 
promotes innovation and entrepreneurship development in rural areas of the country 
for the benefit of potential entrepreneurs.  The Committee, therefore, desires that the 
Report on the third party evaluation of the Scheme may be furnished to the Committee 
for consideration. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
50. The Committee is of the opinion that Ministry needs to improve employability of 
incubates if the schemes are to succeed. The Committ ee is also of the opinion that it would be 
better if ASPIRE is closely linked up with MUDRA, Stand Up and Start Up schemes to provide 
financial assistance to the entrepreneurs. Further, the LBIs should tie up with Self Help 
Groups and women organizations, ITIs and skill development institutions. 
(Para 149) 
 
Action taken 
 
LBIs setup under the scheme are expected to handhold the incubatees/trainees in 
setting up own enterprises. A mechanism will be devised to follow up with the successful 
incubatees and train ees post their training and to connect them with the various schemes of 
financial assistance offered by Government of India/State Governments in order to assist in 
setting up own enterprises and other productive means of employment. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
The aim of any training programme is to benefit its trainee in all aspects related 
to the Training.  But it is also a fact that lack of financial assistance becomes a big 
hurdle for an aspiring trainee to set up an enterprise of his own.  The  Committee, 
therefore, recommends that ASPIRE should be connected to various financial assistance 
schemes such as MUDRA Scheme so that incubates can avail financial assistance and 
become successful entrepreneurs.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
51. The Committee recommends that more LBIs/TBIs should be set up by the Ministry to 
overcome the problems of unemployment, poverty, drudgery and migration which are still 
rampant in rural areas of the country.  The Committee also recommends that Ministry of 
MSME shoul d expedite the sanctioning and setting up of the targeted number of LBIs and 
TBIs across the country and also simplify the technical and procedural formalities which are 
hindering the whole process. 
 
(Para 150) 
 
36 
 

 
Action Taken 
 
A review of the scheme will be taken up at the Ministry in consultation with functional 
LBIs and other institutions/Govt. Departments and necessary modifications in the scheme will 
be done to set up the targeted LBIs/TBIs. 
 
In order to make the scheme of setting up of LBI attrac tive for institutions across the 
Country, budgetary provision, for meeting out recurring expenditure, including training fee 
for initial few years (say five years), may be made in the ASPIRE Scheme. Further it is 
informed that NSIC would be interested in s etting up more number of LBIs at appropriate 
locations on case to case basis, in case built up space is provided free of cost by the respective 
State Governments and budgetary provision for meeting out the recurring expenditure for 
initial few years are made available to NSIC under ASPIRE. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
Unemployment is one of the major problems the youth is facing now -a-days and 
the Covid -19 pandemic has worsened the situation to a large extent.  The Committee 
reiterates its earlier r ecommendation that more LBIs/TBIs should be set up by the 
Ministry to overcome the problems of unemployment and migration of workforce from 
the rural areas of the country. More budgetary provisions should be made to set up 
more and more LBIs and TBIs acros s the country along with simplifying the technical 
and procedural formalities so that more rural youth can take benefit of these LBIs/TBIs, 
which can be helpful in solving the problem of unemployment to certain extent in rural 
areas. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
52. The Committee recommends that awareness camps should also be 
organized/undertaken by the Ministry in rural areas to create awareness among rural 
population in general and among potential artisans in particular regarding these LBIs/TBIs 
and other useful schemes implemented by the Ministry. 
(Para 151) 
 
Action Taken 
 
Awareness campaigns are being organsied at different parts of the country to 
encourage SC/ST entrepreneurs to avail the benefits provided under National SC/ST Hub. In 
FY 2019-20, 71 awareness campaigns were organized under National SC/ST Hub. Moreover, 
National SC -ST Hub Offices (NSSHOs) shall be advised to organize more awareness 
campaigns, particularly in rural areas and Aspirational Districts.        
 
Field offices of Ministry viz. KVIC, Coir Board, Technology Centers and Tool Rooms 
under O/o DC (MSME) will be entrusted with the task to organize awareness camps, etc., 
with focus in rural areas.  
 
37 

The various clusters approved and being operationalized under SFURTI, PMEGP units be ing 
set up and other such beneficiaries, artisans, general public will be informed of the role of 
LBIs/TBIs in promoting the growth of rural entrepreneurship and economy, in particular. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
The Ministry of MSME runs various schemes for benefit of the people.  However, 
due to lack of awareness, the people are not able to take benefit out of the Schemes.  The 
Committee is of the opinion that campaigns should be organized in order to generate 
awareness about the Schemes in the rural area for benefit of the people and their gainful 
employment.  Smart phones may be considered as a medium of generating awareness 
among the youth in rural areas, particularly in respective mother tongue. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
53. The Committee observes that under National SC/ST Hub, the Actual Expenditure has 
always been less than the BE. The Committee is concerned about the under -utilization of 
allocated funds for the marginalized communities. The Committee recommends that special  
efforts need to be made to improve the situation diligently and the Ministry should set up a 
dedicated monitoring cell for this purpose under the supervision of a Monitoring Committee. 
The Committee would also like to know the reasons for continuously pro jecting inflated 
demands and thereafter underutilization of funds every year and why the SC/ST entrepreneurs 
are not able to reap the benefits of the scheme specifically designed for them.   
(Para 165) 
 
Action Taken  
 
Under National SC -ST Hub, a number of initiatives have been introduced for 
providing support to the SC/ST entrepreneurs for capacity building and making them 
competitive. One of the important interventions is Special Credit Linked Capital Subsidy 
(SCLCSS) @ 25% to the SC/ST MSEs. It is aimed to enhance entrepreneurship among SC/ST 
community and also capacity building of existing entrepreneurs so that they may become part 
of the supply chain of CPSEs. It is being implemented by the O/o DC -MSME. Though this 
intervention was introduced in May 2017 , it could become operational only w.e.f December 
2019 onward after the revision of guidelines of CLCSS issued by Office of DC -MSME 
containing the provisions relating to SCLCSS. 
 
The implementation of National SC/ST Hub is being reviewed at various levels from 
time to time. It is expected that the entire funds allocated under National SC/ST Hub in BE 
2020-21 will be utilized. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
National SC/ST Hub is a scheme which was introduced by the Government as a 
welfare measure for the marginalized groups of the society.  
38 
 

But scarcity/underutilization of funds ; lack of awareness among the SC/ST candidates 
about the scheme ; and  technical & procedural difficulties etc.  often act as stumbling 
blocks in the proper implementation of the Scheme.   
 
The Committee , therefore,  recommends that efforts should be made by the 
Ministry/NSIC for creating awareness among SC/ST candidates about the National 
SC/ST Hub scheme, proper budget utilization is ensured and all the technical and 
procedural difficulties should be removed, which are hindering the progress of the 
scheme. The Committee may be apprised of the outcome and progress of the Scheme. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
39 
 

CHAPTER-IV 
 
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the Committee desire further 
comments of the Ministry 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
54. The Committee recommends that MSMEs should be allowed to have only one unified 
GST registration which is applicable in all states. With respect to the sharing of Taxes 
between Central and State Governments, it should be done at the back end as the Government 
already has all the information in this regard. 
         (Para 29) 
 
Action Taken 
 
The issue is being examined. This issue has to be taken up with the Department of 
Revenue for placing the same before the GST Council. 
 
Provision of requirement of registration in different states where the MSME is 
located/liable to pay GST has been recommended by the GST Council, which is a 
Constitutional body and comprises of Central G overnment, State Governments and 
Governments of UT with legislature. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
55. The Committee recommends that multiple registrations with multiple government 
agencies for various purposes should be done away with for MSMEs. Inter -Ministries 
coordination should be improved to bring out one registration to carry out all business 
activities including exports, tax and day -to-day business activities to improve ease of doing 
business for MSMEs. 
         (Para 30) 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
The recommen dation needs to be examined with inputs from all other Ministries/ 
Departments. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
56. The Committee further recommends that steps should be taken so that the MSEs could 
obtain collateral free loans from designated Banks under the  CLCS-TU Scheme in the same 
lines as given under CGTMSE Scheme to encourage more and more entrepreneurs to avail 
the benefits of the scheme and upgrade their technology for quality products. 
 
(Para 133) 
 
 
40 

 
Action Taken 
 
Ministry of MSME will consult the  Ministry of Finance and Reserve Bank of India to 
explore the possibility in this regard. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
57. During examination of DFG 2020 -21, the Committee was apprised of the fact that 
partial collateral had been introduced under CGTMSE Sc heme and that a portal is likely to 
be developed by April 2020 which would appraise loan proposal upfront, and give a rating. 
This rating would bring down the risk perception level of the lending Bank Branch Manager. 
The Committee recommends that the Minis try may launch the proposed Portal expeditiously 
and also apprise the Committee of the enhancement in the off -take in the Scheme, if any, post 
the launch of the Portal. 
 
(Para 134) 
Action Taken 
 
Such a portal was being developed by SIDBI and it is independ ent of the Credit 
Guarantee Scheme of this Ministry implemented through CGTMSE. Ministry will take up this 
issue with SIDBI. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
58. The Committee also observes that the procurements by the CPSEs from the SC/ST and 
Women entrepreneurs, as mandated under the Public Procurement Policy, are much below 
than the sub -quota of 4% and 3% respectively. Even many of the CPSEs have not organised 
Vendor Development Programmes (VDPs) to sensitize the SC/ST entrepreneurs. The 
Committee recommends that sufficient number of VDPs be organised along with buyer -seller 
meets for the benefit of SC/ST and Women entrepreneurs. 
(Para 144) 
Action Taken 
 
Noted. The Ministry will communicate the observation of the committee to all the 
CPSEs and also to the MSME-Development Institutes under Ministry of MSME, located in 
States. 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
59. Since delayed payments to MSEs have been a longstanding issue, the Committee also 
recommends that more MSEFC should be constituted in all the states to r esolve the problem 
of delayed payments expeditiously. Besides, the MSEs should be made aware of the benefits of 
the newly introduced TReDS Platform, wherein bills are paid on a fast track basis. 
(Para 145) 
 
 
41 
 

Action Taken 
 
 The Ministry of MSME has alre ady furnished its suggestions to the Chief Secretary of 
all States/UTs to create MSEFCs at Divisional Level. The States like Maharashtra, Karnataka, 
Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Punjab and Odisha already have more than one MSEFCs in the 
respective States. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
60. The Committee is of the view that the Government Purchase scheme may be amended 
so as to reduce the P erformance Bank Guarantee/security deposit requirement to 10% for 
Micro Enterprises, 20% for Small Enterprises and 30% for Mediu m Enterprises compared to 
the P erformance Bank Guarantee required from non -MSMEs. It is also suggested that 
Medium Industry should also be granted the preferential procurement facility and to pay 25% 
of the Earnest Money Deposit/Bid Bond & tender charges as specified in the tenders. Besides, 
priority sector lending target for micro enterprises from current 7.5% of Adjusted Net Bank 
Credit may be enhanced to at least 12%. 
(Para 146) 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
Noted. An appropriate suggestion would be sent to the Department of Expenditure, 
Ministry of Finance, Government of India, for further necessary action. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
61. LBIs under NSIC serving single window system for new enterprises and has been a 
source of employment. Further, NSIC through its Incubation Centres provides training to the 
prospective entrepreneurs in the manufacturing as well as service sector for skill development 
and employment purposes. The Committee recommends that more Incubation Centres should 
be established in cooperation with State Governments so that training on conventional as well 
as hi -tech trades are imparted to entrepreneurs for their skill development in areas of 
business operation for gainful employment. 
(Para 159) 
Action Taken 
 
In order to make the scheme of se tting up of LBI attractive for institutions across the 
Country, budgetary provision, for meeting out recurring expenditure, including training fee 
for initial few years (say five years), may be made in the ASPIRE Scheme. Further, it is 
informed that NSIC w ould be interested in setting up more number of LBIs at appropriate 
locations on case to case basis, in case built up space is provided free of cost by the respective 
State Governments and budgetary provision for meeting out the recurring expenditure for 
initial few years are made available to NSIC under ASPIRE. 
 
 
42 
 

Recommendation/Observation 
 
62. The Committee observes that NSIC through its Vendor Development Programmes 
sensitize and facilitate MSEs, including SC/ST enterprises, to become qualified vendors to 
public sector enterprises and other Government Departments as per the provision of 25% 
mandatory procurement under Public Procurement Policy. Of this, 4% should be from SC/ST 
MSEs. Also, during its visit to Kolkata, Hyderabad and Mumbai in Janua ry, 2020, the 
Committee found that while the PSUs and Government procurement from MSEs has been 
gradually improving, procurement from SC/ST units is negligible. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that there should be more Vendor Development Programmes org anised to 
popularize Public Procurement Policy among MSEs including SC/ST and Women 
entrepreneurs. 
(Para 167) 
 
Action Taken  
 
National Schedule Caste and Schedule Tribe Hub was launched to provide 
professional support to SC/ST entrepreneurs to fulfill the obligations under the Central 
Government Public Procurement Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises Order 2012, adopt 
applicable business practices and leverage the Stand up India initiatives.   
 
In order to fulfill Public Procurement Policy mandate & to expedite and encourage the 
SC/ST enterprises to be part of public procurement process, NSIC has been organizing 
Vendor Development Programmes (VDPs) for SC/ST entrepreneurs under National SC/ST 
Hub in coordination with CPSEs/Central Ministries and local in dustry associations. These 
VDPs are aimed to provide a common platform for potential vendors from SC -ST MSEs and 
buyer CPSEs where participating MSEs get to know about vendor registration procedures, 
documentation, items being procured and expectation with  respect to the Qualifying 
Requirements. CPSEs get the opportunity to explore new vendors to increase their vendor 
base. More number of such VDPs would be conducted in future. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
63. During 2019-20 (till December, 2019), 4548 unit s have availed testing services from 
these centers. However, the Committee was informed by the representatives of Associations 
during consideration of DFG 2020 -21 that exorbitant rates are charged from MSMEs for 
testing their products for quality certifica tion etc. which is difficult for them to pay as most of 
them face the problem of working capital shortage. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that Testing & Certifications should be made convenient and cheaper for MSMEs. It is 
required that a mechanism/t ie-up should be developed that testing can be done at Indian 
Centres whereas certificates for the same test could be issued from various global testing 
centres, which are acceptable in respective countries/regions. Alternatively, Indian Testing 
Certificates should have global acceptance. Besides, MSMEs should be given subsidies for 
testing facilities in the country. The Committee further recommends that the setting up of Tool 
Rooms and Technology Centres can be explored under the Public -Private Partnership (PPP) 
model. 
(Para 170) 
43 

Action Taken 
 
Information in respect of Hub & Spoke Division on Para 170 of the report mentions 
that: 
 
"The Committee further recommends that the setting up of Tool Rooms and 
Technology Centres can be explored under the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) model." 
 
In this regard it is mentioned that: 
 
(i) In the year 2008 , a new scheme was launched for setting up of mini tool rooms under PPP 
mode. The scheme did not take off and was discontinued. 
(ii) Exploring the PPP model was also approved in the EFC of new scheme for "Setting up of 
20 technology centres and 100 extension centres" at an estimated cost of Rs 6000 crore. A 
team of NITI Aayog experts visited various tool rooms and later on it was deduced that setting 
up of tool rooms (Technology Centers) under PPP model may not be feasible. The reasons can 
be that ROI (return on investment) is not as much as expected by private sector because of the 
non-repetitive work. 
(iii) NITI Aayog concurred to the view that technology centres be set up as government of 
India institutions. 
 
It is to submit that office of DCMSME had recently invited Expression of interest in 
March 2020 from various organizations / Industry Association for submitting proposals to 
establish new Technology Centres in PPP mode. The received proposals are being analysed 
for possible way forward in establishing Technology Centres in PPP mode.

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on  
Industry, having been authorized by the Committee, hereby present  this Three Hundred 
and First Report on Action Taken Notes furnished by the Depart ment of Public 
Enterprises (Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises) on the 
recommendations/observations contained in the Committee’s Two Hundred and Ninety 
Eighth Report on the Demands For Grants (2020 -21) pertaining to Department of Public 
Enterprises. 
 
2.  I, thank the Department of Public Enterprises  (Ministry of Heavy Industries and 
Public Enterprises) for furnishing the Action Taken Notes on the recommendatio ns 
contained in the Committee’s Two Hundred and Ninety Eighth Report. 
 
3.  The Committee in its meeting held on the  16th October, 2020 considered and 
adopted the report. 
  
 
 
 
 
 
New Delhi 
October  16, 2020 
Asvina 24, 1942 (Saka) 
 
Dr. K. Keshava Rao 
Chairman 
Department -related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Industry 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 (ii) 

 1 
REPORT 
 
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry 
of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises (Department of Public Enterprises) on the 
recommendations contained in the Committee‟s Two H undred and Ninety- Eighth Report on the 
Demands for Grants (2020-21) pertaining to Department of Public Enterprises. 
 
2.  Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public 
Enterprises (Department of Public Enterprises) in respect of the recommenda tions contained in 
the 298th Report. These have been categorized as follows: 
 
Chapter-I    The recommendations/observations,  which  have  been accepted by the Ministry. 
 
The Committee is pleased to observe  that the Ministry has accepted its 
recommendations as mentioned in the Chapter – I of the Report.  
 
 Chapter-II-  The recommendations/observations  which  the  Committee  does  not  desire to  
   pursue further in view of the Government's replies. 
 
In respect of these recommendations, the Committee is co nvinced with the logic 
and explanation advanced by the Ministry and therefore does not want to pursue 
them further for the present. 
 
 Chapter-III-  The recommendations/observations  in  respect of  which   the Committee has not  
   accepted replies of the Ministry and desires the Ministry to review their replies. 
 
The Committee is not convinced with the replies of the Ministry in respect of 
recommendations contained in Chapter – III and desires that the Ministry in the 
light of further recommendations/obser vations of the Committee , furnish 
comments/explanations thereof. 
 
  Chapter-IV-  The recommendations/observations  in  respect of  which  the  Committee desire  
   further comments of the Ministry. 
 
In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter -IV, the M inistry has either 
furnished the interim replies, therefore, the Committee desires that the Ministry 
may furnish Action Taken Notes in respect of recommendations categorized in 
Chapter-IV in detail and to the point, as per the intention and spirit of the 
recommendations of the Committee. 
 
3. The details of the Action Taken Replies of the Ministry and further recommendations/ 
observations of the Committee thereon wherever found necessary are given in the succeeding 
pages. 
 
 
 

 2 
 
CHAPTER – I 
 
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN 
ACCEPTED BY THE MINISTRY 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1. The Committee takes note with satisfaction that the objective of the RDC Scheme 
to keep senior management of CPSEs abreast of the latest developments in corporate 
governance, Corporate Social Responsibility Laws, financial matters, Accounting 
Standards, organization and management etc. is being met with the kind of training 
programmes and workshops being conducted by DPE. The Committee notes that 
utilization under RDC Scheme  for 2017 -18 is almost 100% & for 2018 -19, it is 92%. 
However, during 2019 -20, the actual utilization till 31.12.2019 stood at 41%. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that DPE should continue to make efforts to conduct 
more number of training programmes & workshops under RDC scheme in 2020 -21 so 
that the budget allocation can be used optimally. 
                                                                                                                           (Para No 34) 
Action Taken Replies 
 The Committee has observed that utilization under RDC Scheme for 2017 -18 is 
about 100% and for the year 2018 -19 it is 92%.  The Committee has advised that the 
budget allocation should be utilized 100% under RDC Scheme.   
 The recommendation would be duly consid ered for the year 2020 -21 taking into 
account the directions issued by the Government on expenditure management. 
DPE has been conducting training programmes under RDC scheme as per training 
calendar approved for a year.   For the year 2020 -21 more numbers o f training 
programmes may be approved in respect of DPE. 
DPE has been keeping management of CPSEs abreast of latest developments in 
Corporate Social Responsibilities (CSR) by conducting workshops and conferences. A 
workshop on implementation of Corporate S ocial Responsibility by CPSEs in 
Aspirational Districts in Education, Healthcare & Nutrition sectors to discuss the best 
practices, challenges and means to resolve the same was organized by DPE on 3.3.2020 
at New Delhi. The workshop was attended by partici pants from CPSEs, concerned 
Ministries/Departments, District officials of few aspirational districts and implementing 
agencies. Further, it is proposed to organise similar workshops during 2020 -21 on CSR 
under RDC Scheme of the Department.   
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2. The Committee notes with satisfaction that there has been almost 100% utilization 
of the budget allocation under CRR Scheme.  The Committee is, however, of the view that 

 3 
the real achievement of the scheme can be gauged from the number of VRS/ VSS optees/ 
dependants getting re -deployed after availing the skill training.  DPE in their Annual 
Report has stated that during the year 2018 -19, an allocation of Rs.3.96 crore (RE) was 
made available for the CRR scheme.  2000 VRS/ VSS/ dependents we re trained and 924 
were re-deployed (self/ wage employment) which is 46.2%.  The same has been the trend 
in the previous years also.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that re -deployment of 
the trained VRS/ VSS optees/ dependents should be given equal we ightage along with 
their counselling and retraining.  The Committee also recommends that enhancement in 
the redeployment rate of VRS/ VSS optees be perceived by DPE with the association of 
NSDC.  The Committee notes that „Job Fairs‟ have been held in the S tate of Jharkhand 
and West Bengal by the NSDC for the beneficiaries in order to enhance re -deployment.  
The Committee suggests  that more job fairs may be organized in other States as well, 
especially the North Eastern States to promote re-deployment. 
 (Para No 39) 
Action Taken Replies 
 Basic objective of the CRR scheme is to provide redeployment opportunities 
through wage employment /self -employment after skill training in job oriented trades. 
Enhancement of redeployment rate is being perceived with NSDC‟s  association. During 
the last three years viz. 2016-17 to 2018 -19, 5576 persons were trained and 3190 were 
redeployed with an average redeployment rate of 57.2%. The final figure for 2018 -19 
reflects 64% redeployment through skill training in sectors like Healthcare, Electronics, 
Retail Associates, Automotive, Food Processing, Plumbing, Handicrafts, Logistics, I.T   
etc. As advised by the Committee, NSDC will be asked to hold more number of „Job 
Fairs‟. 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
3. The CAPEX increases pro ductivity of PSEs thereby improving economic growth.  
CAPEX by PSEs also contribute to fixed assets creation in the economy.  The 
Government has already directed Maharatna & Navratna companies to review and 
enhance their CAPEX.  The Committee, therefore, d esires that DPE may encourage 
CPSEs to increase their CAPEX through regular monitoring as it is also a parameter for 
MoU evaluation. The committee recommends to conduct outreach programmes to 
sensitise CPSEs to leverage their net worth for infusion into their CAPEX fund.   
(Para No 44) 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 DPE regularly monitors the CAPEX achievement of select CPSEs and furnish 
report of the same to PMO every month. The recommendation of the Hon‟ble committee 
to conduct outreach programmes to sensitise CP SEs to leverage their net worth for 
infusion into their CAPEX fund has been noted for compliance.   
 
 

 4 
 
CHAPTER–II 
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE 
COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE FURTHER IN VIEW OF 
THE GOVERNMENT'S REPLIES 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee is aware that CPSEs in India are undergoing rapid changes and have 
to contribute towards the twin objective of economic development and social cause, within 
the rules and guidelines framed by Government of India. CPSEs are also e xpected to remain 
competitive and generate profit in a highly globalised and market environment. Under such 
circumstances, it is very challenging for CPSEs to show impressive performances. The 
Committee is also aware of the fact that all CPSEs give utmost importance to critical 
performance indicators including R & D, technology upgradation etc. in order to improve 
their performance. The Committee also observes that as the Nodal Department for all 
CPSEs, DPE has been entrusted with a huge responsibility to f ulfill. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the guidelines being framed by the DPE should be in unison with 
the rapid changes the CPSEs are going through. Further, the guidelines should enable 
CPSEs to stand on their own and prove their worth in the expending globalised and market 
economy. The committee further recommends that DPE being the formulator of general 
policy guidelines affecting CPSEs should have a full-fledged the R&D wing of its own to aide 
and advice the CPSEs to achieve the desired goal as explained above. 
 (Para No. 13) 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 DPE has taken various steps to strengthen CPSEs such as helping CPSEs become 
financially self -sustaining, making their presence felt in the expanding global market 
economy, export substitution etc. To facilitate this, the Department of Public Enterprises 
(DPE) has taken the following measures which inter alia  include, (i) introduction of 
Maharatna, Navratna and Miniratna schemes envisaging delegation of financial and 
operational powers to Boards of such CPSEs, (ii) thrust on performance improvement 
through regular evaluation under the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) mechanism,  
(iii) professionalization of Boards of CPSEs and strengthening corporate governance 
framework,  etc. The Boards of Maharatn a, Navratna and Miniratna CPSEs have been 
delegated financial and operational powers in the areas of capital expenditure, investment 
in joint ventures/ subsidiaries, entering technology joint ventures or strategic alliances, 
raising of debts, etc. Further, the Department of Public Enterprises on 29 th October, 2015 
issued guidelines for “Streamlining the mechanism for revival and restructuring of sick/ 
incipient sick and weak Central Public Sector Enterprises: General principles and 

 5 
mechanism of restructurin g". These guidelines are to be implemented by the concerned 
administrative Ministries/ Departments. These guidelines provide mechanism to the 
administrative Departments/Ministries for monitoring sickness, identifying the sub -
optimal performing CPSEs and ta king pre -emptive corrective actions to check onset of 
sickness and take appropriate steps to put the CPSEs back to good financial health. The 
guidelines also provide principles on which administrative Ministries/ Departments draw 
revival/ restructuring pla ns of their CPSEs. DPE has been sensitizing the administrative 
Ministries/ Departments of CPSEs from time to time to take pre -emptive measures in 
accordance with the said guidelines.   
As the CPSEs are under the control of sectoral/ line Ministries, the co ncerned 
sectoral/line Ministries are better placed to take steps to address the issues affecting the 
performance of the CPSEs under their domain, keeping in view the problems faced by 
particular sectors. 
  
Recommendation/ Observation 
5. The Committee finds  that during 2018 -19, the total BE of Rs.20.44 crore was 
increased to Rs. 21.44 crore in RE whereas the AE stood at 21.20 crores. For  the year 
2019-20, both BE & RE were 22.64 crore and the AE for the year till 31.12.2019 is Rs. 
15.96 crore. The Committee appreciates that the Department has managed almost 100% 
fund utilisation of RE during 2018 -19 and 70.49% during 2019 -20 till 31.12.2019. The 
Committee hopes that the Department will optimally utilise the fund allocation in the 
remaining quarter of the yea r. While examining the Head wise budgetary provisions for 
2020-21, the Committee observed that the largest allocation has been made under the 
head „Secretariat Economic Services‟. Out of the total allocated funds of 24.15 crore, 
12.98 crore has been given to Non-Scheme head and the Scheme allocation is only 10.5 
crore. The Committee notes that year after year, budget allocation under Non -Scheme 
Head is higher than the Scheme Head. The Committee recommends that allocation of 
funds should be more concentrated on the “Scheme Heads” which in fact, pertains to the 
flagship scheme of the DPE such as CRR and RDC and on the efficient running of which, 
the performance and result-orientation of CPSEs hinges on.   
                                                                                                                                                                        
(Para No 28) 
Action Taken Replies 
 The expenditure of DPE for the year 2019 -20 has been Rs.21.10 crores which is 
93.2% of BE.  DPE has two Sche mes viz. Counselling, Retraining & Redeployment 
(CRR) and Research Development  & Consultancy (RDC) Scheme. Demand of funds 
under CRR during the year 2020 -21 has been kept in consonance with projected 
VRS/VSS figure. 
 
So far as RDC scheme is concerned, DPE  has made all efforts to diversify 
activities for coverage. Besides undertaking   some senior level training of CPSEs, 

 6 
specific activities/studies take place from time to time under RDC. DPE in collaboration 
with IIT Bombay has set up a CSR Study Unit know n as DPE-IITB project at Centre for 
Technology Alternative in Rural Areas (CTARA), IIT Bombay. The CSR Unit will 
undertake PAN - India study of all CSR eligible CPSEs in the country and the impact 
assessment of CSR activities / projects undertaken by CPSEs . A one -day conference on 
“Implementation of CSR in Aspirational Districts by CPSEs in Education, Healthcare and 
Nutrition Sectors – Issues, Challenges and Best Practices”  was organized by DPE on 3rd 
March, 2020 in association with IIT Bombay and NITI Aayog.  
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
6. The Committee notes that MoU system is an important tool that enables DPE to 
evaluate the performance of the management of CPSEs on key selected parameters 
against targets agreed upon so as to improve critical performan ce indicators of the 
organization.  The MoU system also helps CPSEs to upgrade their processes and 
systems, address corporate governance imperatives and improve accountability.  During 
the year 2019 -20, 144 CPSEs have signed MoU with their respective Minis tries/ 
Departments and their performance rating would be evaluated after completion of the 
financial year.  Since Independent Directors of Boards of CPSEs play a key role in 
ensuring good corporate governance, the Committee recommends that MoU system may 
be reviewed to incorporate a new evaluation parameter on „non-filling up of vacant posts 
of Non-Official Directors on the Boards of CPSEs as a deterrent for CPSEs which do not 
take action timely to fill up such vacant posts. 
(Para No 50) 
Action Taken Replies 
 
 In MoU, it is to evaluate the performance of Management in those parameters 
which are within the control of CPSE.  At present, the CPSE have no direct role in the 
process of selection and appointment of Independent Directors.  The proposals for 
appointment of Non -official Directors for CPSEs are initiated by the concerned 
Administrative Ministries/Departments. The selection of Non-official Directors in respect 
of all CPSEs is made by the Search Committee which presently consists of Secretary 
(DoPT), Sec retary (DPE), Secretary of the Administrative Ministry/Department of the 
concerned CPSE and 2 non -official Members. The concerned Administrative 
Ministry/Department appoints the Non -official Directors on the basis of 
recommendations of the Search Committee  after obtaining the approval of Appointments 
Committee of the Cabinet (ACC). Therefore, it may not be feasible to include it in MoU 
process. 

 7 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
7. The Committee notes that Government is keen on disinvestment of CPSEs except 
those belonging to high priority areas such as National Security, Sovereign function at 
arm‟s length & market imperfection and public purpose, as Government doesn‟t want to 
engage itself in Sectors where competitive markets have come of age. However, the 
Committee recommends that to support and strengthen the CPSEs operating in „Priority 
Areas‟ of Business, as identified by NITI Aayog. DPE should play a more pre-active role, 
especially in respect of those CPSEs, which are already doing business in the „Priority 
Areas‟, which need support to excel their performance. In the case of sick, incipient sick 
and weak CPSEs, their concerned Administrative Departments have been vested with the 
responsibility of monitoring their sickness and evolve measures for their reviva l/re-
structuring. The Committee also observed that even through DPE is not mandated to deal 
with matters concerning disinvestment of CPSEs, it issues broad policy guidelines of 
CPSEs. Therefore, the Committee recommends that while disposing of the land of CPSEs 
identified for closure/strategic disinvestment, the applicable guidelines should be 
scrupulously followed. The Committee during the course of examination of the Demands 
for Grants desired to know whether in the „Net Worth‟ of a Company , its total hol ding 
value, including land assets were taken into consideration as per its current market value 
or only its paid -up capital and reserves mode out of its profits were taken into 
consideration.  In case only the latter parameter is considered while assessing  the 
networth of a company, then a policy intervention is the need of the hour, which was to 
be taken up by DPE with the concerned Ministry. Further, the Committee suggest that 
networth of the land of such CPSEs should be calculated as per the prevalent ma rket 
rates. 
                                                                                                                                 (Para 57) 
 
Action Taken Replies 
DPE as per its mandate continue to support CPSEs including in the „Priority 
Areas‟ of Business through various capacity building programmes, laying down of 
guidelines on corporate governance, delegation of powers under „Ratna‟ Scheme, 
monitoring of CAPEX of Select CPSEs and regular Performance Evaluation through MoU 
System.  DPE has also written to the concerned administrative Ministries/ Departments to 
advise their respective CPSEs for bench marking with national/ international peers to 
cover productivity, efficiency with quality standards and areas.  
 
With regard to the recommendation o f the Committee on disposal of land, it is 
submitted that the implementation of the guidelines regarding sale and disposal of land of 
CPSEs approved for closure is done by the CPSE and the concerned administrative 

 8 
Ministry/ Department. Therefore, the recommendation of the committee has been brought 
to the notice of the administrative Ministries/ Departments. 
 
With regard to the issue of net worth, it is submitted that Section 2 (57) of the 
Companies Act 2013, defines the “net worth”. The Companies Act  2013 was passed by 
the Act of p arliament. The Companies Act is administered by Ministry of Corporate 
Affairs.  It defines “net worth” of a company as “the aggregate value of the paid -up share 
capital and all reserves created out of the profits, securities premi um account and debit or 
credit balance of profit and loss account, after deducting the aggregate value of the 
accumulated losses, deferred expenditure and miscellaneous expenditure not written off, 
as per the audited balance sheet, but does not include res erves created out of revaluation 
of assets, write -back of depreciation and amalgamation.” Net worth is different from 
“market value” of the company. 
 
Companies follows the accounting standard while preparation and presenting their 
financial statements. Acc ounting Standard (AS) 10/Indian Accounting Standard (IND 
AS) 16 on “Plant, Property, and Equipment (PPE)” are the extant Accounting Standards 
dealing with the Plant, Property, and Equipment which is represented by different class of 
assets, such as land, l and & Building, machinery, etc.  As per the standard, the value of 
fixed assets, including land, can be either at historical cost or revalued cost in the Annual 
Accounts. If an asset is revalued, the entire class of PPE to which that asset belongs 
should be revalued. But for the purpose of book of accounts, if it is valued at a particular 
point of time, then it will be the same value until and unless it is revalued.   
 
Further, as per the Accounting Standards, when fixed asset is revalued, the excess of 
market value over the book value on the date of revaluation is not considered as a normal 
profit earned in the normal course of business/operations and is credited to revaluation 
reserves. Since it is not created out of net profits - i.e. by appropriation out  of the net 
profit, it is excluded in calculation of networth. Therefore, the networth is not a market 
value. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 9 
 
 
CHAPTER–III 
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE 
COMMITTEE HAS NOT ACCEPTED THE REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY AND 
DESIRES THE MINISTRY TO REVIEW THEIR REPLIES 
 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
8. The Committee notes that the total No. of CPSEs stood at 348 during 2018 -19, 
whereas the figure for 2017 -18 showed 339 CPSEs only.  Therefore, the No. of CPSEs 
has increased by 9 which shows 2.65% growth over the previous year.  However, the No. 
of operating CPSEs has reduced from 258 during 2017 -18 to 249 during 2018 -19, 
showing a decrease in growth by 3.49%.  Further most of the indicators such as the paid-
up capital, Capital Employ ed, Networth, Investment, Reserves & Surplus total turnover, 
overall profit, Foreign Exchange Earnings, etc., indicate a steady increase from 2016 -17 
to 2018-19. 
 
However, indicators such as Dividend paid, regular employment in numbers, 
Market Capitalisation, etc., have shown a steady decline from the year 2016 -17 to 2018-
19.  The Committee observes that one of the main objectives for setting up of PSEs was to 
create employment opportunities in the country.  However, the macro -view of the 249 
operating CPSE s for the last 3 years show gradual decline in number of regular 
employees.  As per the information furnished by DPE as part of examination of Demands 
for Grants 2020-21, there is a reduction of 55,560 employees from 2017-18 to 2018-19. 
 
However, as per th e Public Enterprises Survey 2018 -19 brought out by DPE, 
CPSEs across Sectors provided employment to 15,14,064 people as on 31.03.2019, 
including casual workers and contract workers, as against 15,54,967 as on 31.03.2018.  
As per the Survey, there is a reduction of 40,903 employees (2.63%) in total No. of people 
employed by CPSEs including casual and contract employees. 
 
The Committee notes that there is a mismatch in the figures regarding number of 
employees in CPSEs as shown in the written submission made by DPE before the 
committee and the Public Enterprises Survey 2018 -19.  However, it is a fact that there is 
a gradual decline in number of regular employees in CPSEs.  The Committee therefore 
recommends that CPSEs should be encouraged to fulfil their Socia l Objective and 
provide more permanent employment to people, instead of engaging personnel on casual 
and contract basis. 
 

 10 
 
The Committee also observed during the course of examining the Demands for 
Grants that a number of PSUs, even the profit making Mahar atnas fail to fill up 
vacancies of personnel and many a time, such vacancies are filled by hiring of 
superannuated employees on contractual basis, to fill up the vacancies, which is not a 
healthy trend. The Committee recommends that DPE should take steps t o encourage 
CPSEs and Ministries concerned to desist from this practice and employ young minds in 
the vacancies, on regular basis, so that CPSEs can gain from the new concepts and 
interests evinced by such young minds and become globally competitive. 
(Para No 20) 
Action Taken Replies 
 In compliance of the Recruitment / employment of personnel to the posts below 
Board level are done by the Management of respective Central Public Sector Enterprises 
(CPSEs) as per their Recruitment/ Human Resource Policy. The necessary qualification 
and eligibility criterion for posts below Board level is also decided by the respective 
CPSE as per their H.R. Policy.   In compliance of the recommendation, the Department 
has written to all administrative Ministries on 6th April, 2020 to sensitize all CPSEs under 
their respective administrative jurisdiction to put in place a system of „Succession 
Planning‟ and to ensure that all vacant positions related to core activities of CPSEs are 
filled through regular incumbents.  
 
Further Recommendations/ Observations 
  
The Committee notes from the Government's reply that the DPE is silent on 
the observation of the Committee regarding the mismatch in the figures about the 
number of employees in CPSEs as presented before the Committee and the f igures 
shown in the Public Enterprises Survey 2018 -19.  The Committee desires that the 
discrepancy in data be clarified and also rectified. 
 
 Further, the Committee acknowledges the fact that the 
Recruitment/employment of Personnel to the Post below Board level are done by the 
Management of the  respective Central Pubic Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) as per 
their recruitment/Human Resources Policy that lays down the necessary 
qualification and eligibility Criteria Post -wise depending upon their nature of work 
and requirement.  The Committee wh ile appreciating the efforts taken up by the 
Department to sensitise CPSEs through their administrative Ministries, to put in 
place a System of "Succession Planning" for filling up vacant position s in CPSEs, 
also expect the  DPE, being the Nodal Department of all CPSEs with regard to 
overall Human Resource Management, to act as a watchdog to ensure timely filling 
up of all vacancies arising from time to time, by conducting surveys at regular 
intervals rather than putting the onus on the administrative Ministries alone. 
 
 
 

 11 
Recommendation/Observation 
9. The Committee is aware that professionalization of boards of CPSEs is extremely 
essential for making CPSEs more competitive and viable in the emerging market 
economy. It is also essential for ensuring good corporate governance. In its 290 th Report 
the Committee had inter alia recommended that the process of filling up the regular 
Board level vacancies should be initiated by the CPSEs at least one year before vacancy 
actually occurs so that there is no gap between the anticipated vacancy and recruitment. 
Subsequently, the Department of PE in its ATR had informed that the said 
recommendation had been forwarded to Public Sector Enterprises Selection Board 
(PSEB) under the DOPT for nec essary action, as it initiates the selection process for 
filling up of Board level posts in CPSEs one year in advance of occurrence of anticipated 
vacancies. However, it is saddening to note that around 313 positions out of 701 
positions of non -official Di rectors are at present vacant in various CPSEs. The 
Committee therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation that the process for filling up 
of vacant post of regular non -official Directors in various CPSEs should be initiated one 
year before the actual occurrence of the vacancy to avoid delay in filling up of vacancies. 
The Committee also recommends that DPE should follow up the matter with PESB and 
concerned administrative ministries and report the outcome to the Committee. The 
Committee further recomme nds that the existing 313 vacant positions of Non -official 
Directors in various CPSEs should be filled up expeditiously to ensure good corporate 
governance. 
 (Para No 61) 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 Public Enterprises Selection Board has been requested again vi de OM dated 15 th 
April, 2020 to furnish their reply on the matter of timely filling up of vacant positions of 
functional Directors of CPSEs. As regards vacant posts of non -official (Independent) 
Directors on the Boards of CPSEs, the Department takes note o f the concern expressed 
by the Hon‟ble Committee and submits that necessary steps are being taken to fill up 
vacant positions of Independent Directors on the Boards of CPSEs. 
 
Further Recommendations/ Observations 
  
The Committee notes the reply given by DPE and desires to know the specific 
measures being taken to fill up the vacancies of non -official (Independent) Directors 
in the Boards of CPSEs, expeditiously. 
 
 The Committee is, however constrained to express is displeasure in the 
inordinate delay in fi lling up the vacancies of Directors (both functional as well as 
Independent) on the Boards of CPSEs despite the several recommendations in this 
regard made by the Committee earlier.  These vacancies would have a cascading 

 12 
effect on the effective functionin g of CPSEs and also indicate lack of vision, 
planning and good corporate governance.  The Committee, therefore, recommend s 
that DPE should follow up the  matter with Public Enterprises  Selection Board, 
Department of Personnel & Training vigorously and moni tor the progress regularly 
so that the existing vacancies of functional Directors  in the Boards of CPSEs can be 
filled up expeditiously.  The Committee would also like the Department to report 
back to the Committee. 
  
Recommendation/ Observation 
10. The C ommittee notes that all CPSEs meeting the criteria specified in Section 
135 of Comp any Act, 2013 are mandated to undertake CSR activities in project mode 
preferably, in the local area of the company's unit, plant or factory as far as possible. 
Wherever it is not possible, the CPSEs are at liberty to undertake the CSR activities 
in any part of the country. Further, as per the latest guidelines for CSR expenditure 
of CPSEs issued by DPE on 10 th December, 2018, a common theme will be identified for 
each year f or undertaking CSR by CPSEs, which should cover 60% of annual CSR 
expenditure and Aspirational Districts have to be given preference.  
However, during the recent Study V isit of the Committee to Hyderabad on 
08/01/2020 the Committee observed that the CSR exp enditure by most of the CPSEs 
were incurred on construction of toilets, contribution to Swachh Bharat Kosh, 
improving existing drinking water facility, health care facilities, etc.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that DPE in co -ordination with admini strative ministries 
should ensure that the CPSEs are aware of the new provisions in the revised 
guidelines such as theme based activity to be undertaken every year, preference to be 
given to Aspirational Districts, etc.  
 
The Committee also recommends that the CPSEs should desist from using CSR 
fund to supplement Government schemes as the objective of CSR fund is to involve 
corporates in discharging their social responsibility with their innovative ideas and 
management skills.  The Committee is also of the c onsidered opinion that the CSR 
expenditure in NE R should be given more weightage.  
 
The Committee feels that the involvement of local representatives such as the 
area MLA/ MLC and MP is of paramount importance in CSR related activities.  The 
Committee, acco rdingly, recommends that area MLA/ MLC and MP should be 
consulted both at the time of selection of CSR projects as well as at their 
implementation stage.  This will go a long way to fulfil the aspirations of residents of 
these areas.  
(Para No. 67) 

 13 
Action Taken Replies 
 Recommendation/ observation made by the Hon'ble Committee has been 
noted. In order to ensure that the CPSEs undertake Corporate Social Responsibility 
(CSR) activities in a focused and theme based manner, the Department of Public 
Enterprises (DPE) has issued guidelines in December, 2018 in line with the 
recommendations of the CPSEs Conclave held in April, 2018.  The guidelines 
provide for 60% of annual CSR expenditure by CPSEs on a specific theme with 
preference to aspirational districts in th e country identified by NITI Aayog.  The 
theme for 2018 -19 was “School Education and Healthcare” whereas for 2019 -20, 
the theme was “School Education, Healthcare and Nutrition”.  The Department of 
Public Enterprises has been sensitizing the CPSEs through v arious meetings, 
conferences, workshops, etc. for undertaking CSR activities in line with the above 
guidelines.   
 
 
Further Recommendations/ Observations 
 
The Committee  appreciates the measures being taken by DPE to sensitise 
CPSEs to undertake CSR activit ies in a focussed and the me based manner in 
accordance with the guidelines issued in December, 2018.  However, the Committee 
notes from the Department's reply that its recommendation for involving local 
representatives such as the area MLAs/MLCs and MPs ha s not been addressed.  
The Committee feels that involving local representatives will help in selecting need 
based projects and the area where such projects are to be implemented, thus  
benefitting a larger population of the area/community.  The Committee, t herefore, 
reiterates its recommendations that DPE may frame guidelines for involving local 
representatives like MLAs, MLCs and MPs right from the initiation process of the  
CSR Projects till the competition thereof.  
 
The Committee further notes that DPE ha s not addressed the following 
recommendations made by the Committee:- 
 
The Committee also recommends that the CPSEs should desist from using 
CSR fund to supplement Government schemes as the objective of CSR fund is to 
involve corporates in discharging thei r social responsibility with their innovative 
ideas and management skills.  The Committee is also of the considered opinion 
that the CSR expenditure in NER should be given more weightage.  
  
The Committee would like to be apprised of the action on the afore said 
recommendations.  
 
  
  

 14 
CHAPTER – IV 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE 
COMMITTEE DESIRE FURTHER COMMENTS OF THE MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
11. The Committee notes that DPE has been able to use the budget allocation under 
RDC Scheme optimally, in the North Eastern Region.  The Committee also notes that 
DPE periodically reviews the CRR scheme to make it more useful to VRS/ VSS optees/ 
dependants.  The scheme, however, will be more meaningful when the trained VRS/ VSS 
optees/ dependants are re -deployed.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates that the 
beneficiaries of a particular area should be imparted training in such skills which are in 
demand and which can be made use for employment in that area.  The Committee cannot 
fathom the fact that year after year, DPE has not been able to utilize the fund allocated 
under CRR in North Eastern Region, due to non -availability of VRS/ VSS optees/ 
dependants in North Eastern Region.  Even though the unutilized funds do not lapse and 
gets tr ansferred to Non Lapsable Pool, it does not reach the beneficiaries, thereby 
hampering the development of the North Eastern Region.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that DPE should re -visit the CRR Scheme and find out ways and means to 
make it more attractive for the VRS/ VSS optees/ dependents of North Eastern Region, so 
that the desired results can be achieved.  Further, quarterly/ mid term review of the 
scheme may be undertaken to improve the utilization of the Scheme.  DPE should also 
sensitise the CPSEs in North Eastern Region which undertake downsizing of employees 
to use the data bank available with them to encourage VRS/ VSS optees/ dependants of 
such CPSEs to make use of the CRR scheme. 
(Para No 42) 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 As already stated in reply to Para 28 that setting up of physical targets under CRR 
scheme depends on number of persons released under VRS/VSS.  The scope of CRR 
scheme has been reviewed from time to time to include dependents of VRS/ VSS optees,

 Regarding NER, DPE has been pursuing with the CPSEs having units in NER  for

sharing the available data bank of VRS/ VSS optees to improve the number of trainees in

Recommendation/Observation 
 
 1.              From the above table as per information furnished by the DHI, it can be seen 
that only a sum of Rs 1489.98 cr as BE is allocated for 2020-21 which is less than 50% of 
the demanded amount. DHI’s flagship scheme like FAME -India has been given very less

Capital goods sector, heavy Engineering & Electrical, Auto sector are very critical to

(para 18) 
 
Action Taken Replies 
Recommendation of the Committee have been forwarded to the relevant 
Ministries ie Committee‟s recommendation on Scrappage Policy which is incentive 
based, has been taken up with MO RTH and issue of reduction of GST has been referred 
to Deptt of Revenue. 
    
Recommendation/Observation 
  
2. Further, during examination of the DFG 2020 -21, some of the Automobile 
Associations had put forth their views/suggestions for revival of the Auto I ndustry from 
the present slump that it is undergoing, by measures such as reduction in import duty for 
lithium ion cell battery which is used for operating the e-vehicles etc. The committee after 
hearing the Associations, recommends that Ministry may take up the following issues 
with the concerned:  
 
(i)         Import duty on lithium ion cells in Batteries, on which e -vehicles are 
being operated, be kept at zero per cent till the Auto Industry revives itself.  
(ii)         levy of uniform road tax across all states.  
 (para 19)  
 
 

 16 
Action Taken Replies 
DHI is pro-active in assisting  OEMs by taking up their concerns with other 
Ministries/Departments. Ministry of Finance has revised the custom duty on the EV 
components to promote local manufacturing of these components.  
Recommendations of the Committee on Zero Import Duty on Li -ion cells in 
batteries, on which e -vehicles are operated and levy on uniform road tax have been 
forwarded to D/o Revenue and MORTH respectively. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
   
3. During course of examination of DFG 2020 -21, it was brought to notice of the 
Committee that DHI has entr usted the task of making three E xpressway fully e -vehicle 
friendly by way of establishing of charging infrastructure at regular intervals to its 
PSUslike BHEL and REIL. These highways are Delhi -Chandigarh, Delhi – Jaipur and 
Mumbai – Pune Expressways. The C ommittee is pleased to note that amongst these, the 
Delhi Chandigarh highways has been declared as the first expressway of the country, 
which is e -vehicle friendly. The committee would like to be apprised of the progress on 
the other proposed highways and the likely date of their completion.  
 (para 37) 
Action Taken Replies 
Progress on the other proposed highways i.e. Delhi – Jaipur and Mumbai – Pune, 
as on 15.5.2020, is as below:  
1. Twenty two charging stations have been installed on the Delhi – Jaipur 
Highway/Expressway and work is in progress for another 10 charging stations.  
2. Eleven charging stations have been installed on the Mumbai – Pune 
Highway/Expressway and work is in progress for another 6 charging stations.    
 
  The installation work for these charging Stations is to be completed within a few 
months after lifting of lock down, due to Covid -19 outbreak. Due to advisories against 
any travel due to Covid  -19, especially in the state of Maharashtra and NCR, it would be 
difficult to indicate date of completion. 
  
It is also submitted that completion of this R&D project may be impacted due to 
COVID-19 pandemic and country -wide lockdown. However, all efforts are being made 
for execution and completion of the project as per schedule. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. From the above submissions of DHI, the Committee observes that the actual total 
cost of the AUSC project has come down to Rs.905 crores instead of th e initially 
estimated cost of Rs.1554 crore. The funding requirement from DHI has been reduced 
from Rs. 900 crore to Rs. 474 crores. Out of which the Govt. has already allocated the 
entire amount of Rs. 474 crore (Rs. 120 crore in 2017 -18,Rs. 220 crore in 2018-19 and 

 17 
Rs. 134 crore in 2019 -20). However the Committee observes that DHI has utilized only 
Rs. 110 crores upto 31.01.2020, a balance of Rs. 24 crores is pending unspent which 
needs to utilized in the remaining period of FY 2019 -20. The Committee also  observes 
from the submissions of DHI that the target date set for completion of the R&D project is 
by the end of September 2020. The Committee recommends that the Department should 
take all out efforts to spend the entire balance of Rs. 24 crores in the F Y 2019-20. The 
Committee also desires to be informed about meeting of expenses upto September 2020 
i.e., the set target date of completion when no provisioning of fund on this account has 
been made in the BE 2020-21. 
(para 60) 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 
The ba lance grant of Rs. 24 cr from Department of Heavy Industry (DHI) 
earmarked for FY 2019 -20 was released to the AUSC Mission Directorate on 28 -02-
2020, and this amount has been transferred/allocated to the three consortium partners. 
The grant will be utilize d by the consortium partners during FY 2020 -21 for carrying out 
R&D phase project activities.  Further, no additional grant from DHI is required for the 
AUSC R&D project during 2020-21. 
 
It is also submitted that completion of this R&D project may be impact ed due to 
COVID-19 pandemic and country -wide lockdown. However, all efforts are being made 
for execution and completion of the project as per schedule. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
5. The Committee notes that the allocated BE 2020 -21 is only Rs 6 crores as  Grants 
in Aid for salaries support to CMTI as against the Projected Budget of Rs 22.00 crores. 
As the fund allotted is just sufficient to meet the salaries of the faculty, the R&D 
programmes are likely to be badly affected. The Committee recommends that t he DHI 
should seek sufficient funds in the RE 2020 -21 for the purpose of R&D programme, for 
developing high tech core manufacturing technologies. 
(para 70) 
 
Action Taken Replies 
The Department released Rs 19.00 crores as Grant in Aid for salaries to CMTI f or 
the Financial Year 2019-20. An amount of Rs.22 crores was the projected expenditure for 
the Grant-in-Aid for salaries for CMTI for the FY 2020-21. The Department will seek the 
remaining funds under this Head in RE 2020-21.  
 
Further, as advised, additional funds will be sought for R & D and development of 
high tech core manufacturing technologies for CMTI under Phase-II of the Capital Goods 
Scheme at the RE 2020-21 stage. 
 

 18 
In addition, DHI is supporting CMTI in their efforts to develop high end 
technologies and infrastructural facilities such as Development of Shuttle less High 
Speed Rapier Loom, Smart Manufacturing and Industry 4.0 Centre, a Precision 
Metrology Lab, Nano Manufacturing Technology Centre, Sensor Technology 
Development Facility, etc. The De partment has released Rs. 85.26 crores in last three 
years for the development of the above technologies and facilities through the Scheme for 
Enhancement of Competitiveness in Indian Capital Goods Sector.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
6. From the above fa cts it is seen that the entire amount of Rs. 469.41 crore for 
undergoing the Revival and Mill Development Plan has been sanctioned/released. 
Though the RMDP was supposed to be completed by December, 2019, the deadline has 
been missed. The DHI in their subm ission has assured that it is likely to take some more 
time for completion. The Committee therefore, expects the RMDP of NEPA to be 
completed soon by fast track monitoring by the Department and report compliance to the 
Committee. 
  
(para 85) 
Action Taken Replies 
The Department of Heavy Industry has constituted a Monitoring Committee under 
the chairmanship of AS&FA, DHI to regularly review the progress of the implementation 
of the RMDP of Nepa Limited. The Department has also constituted a Technical 
Committee with senior experts and engineers from Central Pulp & Paper Research 
Institute (CPPRI), BHEL and Bridge and Roof Co. Ltd to provide technical assistance to 
Nepa Ltd., if required. This team is part of the Department‟s regular review and 
monitoring process for the RMDP. Till date, fourteen meetings of the Review Committee 
have been held.  
 
The announcement of the nationwide lock down due to the 'Covid -19 Pandemic' 
has resulted in all construction work relating to the RMDP stopping for almost 40 days. 
The c oncerned District Administration has recently given permission to NEPA Ltd. to 
resume the RMDP work with stringent conditions and very limited manpower. 
             
The Department shall make best efforts to fast track monitoring as directed by the 
Committee.   
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
7. The Committee observes that some irregularity has been done by BHEL by 
misusing the funds towards extending undue benefits to its employees on account of 
payment of Late Night Snacks Allowance in gross violation to th e extant rules/guidelines 
of DPE. The Committee would like to know the present status of the Audit observation 
and action taken by BHEL and DHI for its settlement. The Committee also desires that 
DHI should issue instructions to all CPSEs under its domain to strictly adhere to the 

 19 
guidelines of DPE and maintain financial propriety in accordance with the laid -down 
policy. 
(para 89) 
Action Taken Replies 
Departure from provisions governing payment of Late Night Snacks Allowance 
(LNSA) was only in respect of Hy derabad Unit of BHEL, and not across the Company. 
The LNSA issue has since been rectified by Hyderabad Unit of BHEL vide its Circular 
issued in April 2018 in line with provision laid down in the Personnel Manual of the 
Company. Accordingly, the concern rai sed in the Audit observation has been suitably 
addressed. It is also confirmed that the provisions laid down in Personnel Manual with 
respect to LNSA are implemented by BHEL in all its Units and for all category of 
employees. Presently, no issue or actiona ble point on this is pending from BHEL‟s side. 
In the past, two Action Taken Notes have been furnished by this Department to the o/o 
C&AG for dropping of this audit para. Now, a fresh Action Taken Note is again being 
sent to C&AG with the request to drop this para.

 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry, having been authorized by the Committee, do hereby present this Three 
Hundred and Third  Report on t he Downturn in Automobile Sector  - Its Impact and 
Measures for Revival.

REPORT 
 
The Indian Automobile Industry comprising automobile and the automotive 
component segments is one of the key contributors to economic growth of India. Being 
deeply integrated with other industrial sectors, it is a major driver of the manufacturing 
Gross Domestic Product (GDP), exports and employment. India is a prime destination for 
many multinational automobile companies with the aspirations of business expansion , 
and the basic advantages that the country provides as an investment destination , includes 
cost-effective operations, efficient and large scale manpower , a fast growing dynamic 
market, since the liberalization of the sector in 1991 , and allowing 100%  FDI through 
automatic route. In Indian Automobile Sector today, there is presence of almost  every 
global auto manufacturer in the country. All categories of vehicles like Two Wheelers, 
Three Wheelers, passenger cars, light commercial vehicles, trucks, buses, tractors, Heavy 
commercial vehicles etc. are produced in India. India is the largest man ufacturer of Two 
Wheelers and Three Wheelers and the fourth  largest manufacturer of passenger cars in 
the world. Further, the manufacturing of automobiles including trucks, buses, cars, three 
wheelers/two wheeler s etc, has risen at a very high pace  in Indi a. Indian Automobile 
Industry today is  a `8.2 lakh crore industry. Presently, the a utomobile industry turnover 
constitutes 7.1% of GDP, 27% of Industrial GDP and 49% of Manufacturing GDP and 
provides about 3.7 crore direct and indirect employment. Besides the current annual sale 
of vehicles is about 26 milli on and 8% of the total exports worth 27 billion USD come 
from the automobile industry. It is also a large contributor to the national exchequer, 
contributing `1.5 lakh crore in the total GST which corres ponds to 15% of the total GST 
collected.  Indian Auto Components Industry is also 57 billion USD i.e. `3.95 lakh crore 
industry. The Indian Auto component turnover constitute 2.3% of GDP an d provides 5 
million employment and exports to the tune of 15-16 billion USD i.e. `1.06 lakh crore. 
2. Agricultural Machinery is mainly dominated by agricultural tractors. Indian 
Tractor Industry is the largest in the world, accounting for the third of the Global 
production. Indian Tractors are gaining acceptance in inter national markets and therefore 
Indian Tractors are exported to US and other countries like Malaysia, Turkey and Africa. 

2 
 
As the cost of tractors in India is cheapest in the world, there is tremendous scope for 
improvement of export of tractors in future.

Automobile production and sales i ndicating negative growth or slowdown in the Auto

associated with the Auto Industry for analysing the causes, impact and for recommending 
remedial measures for reviving the Auto Industry.

12. The Committee in its meeting held on 4 th November, 2019 heard the views of the 
representatives of Auto Industry Associations viz Society of Indian automobile 
Manufacturers (SIAM), Automotive Component Manufacturers Association (ACMA),

invited suggestions f rom these Associations for consideration and to recommend 
remedial measures to revive the auto industry.  The Secretary, Department of Heavy

16. The Committee was also i nformed by the Automobile Sector Associations that 
new hiring of manpower has been stopped in the auto industry sector. Besides, 286 Auto 
Dealers who could not sustain operations i n the downturn of Auto Industry have been 
closed. Further, the production cuts in the Automobile Sector have a percolating negative

automobile spare parts manufacturing.  Auto Industry being the backbone of Indian 
Economy, any strain in the Automobile Sector will have a major impact on the Indian
