clusters are in Khadi, Coir, Handicraft, Handloom, Agro -processing, honey sector etc.  In 2020 -
21, 37 clusters have been approved till 31.12.2020 assisti ng 21,226 artisans. Ministry has 
released an amount of Rs. 127.41 cr. during the year 2020-21 (till 31.12.2020) for implementing 
the activities prescribed in the DPRs such as setting up of Common Facility Centres (CFC), 
procurement of machineries, conducti ng Soft Interventions activities such as marketing 
initiatives, awareness programmes etc.  

24 
 
52. Further, the Committee was informed that 371 clusters have been approved till now and 
only 82 clusters are operational under SFURTI Scheme. The Ministry submitte d that SFURTI is 
an excellent scheme targeted at the welfare of artisans across the farthest areas of the country and 
assured to give prominence to this Scheme.  Besides, the Ministry informed that normally setting 
up of clusters was taking around three years but now it is taking around one plus year. 
53. The Committee notes that the BE for SFURTI Scheme for FY 2020-21 i.e. Rs. 464.85 
crore was reduced at the RE Stage to Rs. 300 crore and the Actual Expenditure was only 
Rs. 192.54 crores till 31 st January, 2021. The Committee also notes that against a projected 
Budget Estimate of Rs. 500 crore for the SFRUTI Scheme for FY 2021 -2022, an allocation 
of only Rs. 170 crore has been made. The Committee expresses its concern over the low 
utilization pattern and red uction in allocations for an important Scheme of the Ministry, 
which is capable of generating employment in a large scale in the rural areas for the 
artisans, particularly during the Covid Pandemic. The Committee recommends that a 
holistic evaluation study of the Scheme may be conducted and based on the said study more 
allocations should be projected by the Ministry at the RE Stage for effective 
implementation of SFURTI Scheme for benefit of the traditional artisans. 
54. The Committee is constrained to note that out of 371 clusters which have been 
approved, only 82 clusters are operational so far. The Committee recommends that the 
process of setting up of SFURTI clusters should be expedited; targets should be set and 
ensure that the approved clusters are completed and become operational within the 
stipulated timeframe for benefit of artisans.   
55. The Committee was apprised by the Ministry that besides 219 Districts, 56 
Aspirational Districts have also been covered under S FURTI. The Committee recommends

in those districts and improve the human dev elopment index. The Ministry may coordinate

56. During the Covid Pandemic induced lockdowns, scores of migrant workers were

Coir Board and Coir Vikas Yojana 
57. The Coir Board is a stat utory body established under the Coir Board Industry Act, 1953 
for promoting overall development of the coir industry and improving the living conditions of 
the workers engaged in this traditional industry. The activities of the Board for development of 
coir industries, inter alia include undertaking scientific, technological and economic research and 
development activities; collecting statistics relating to exports and internal consumption of coir 
and coir products; developing new products and designs; org anizing publicity for promotion of 
exports and internal sales; marketing of coir and coir products in India and abroad; preventing 
unfair competition between producers and exporters; assisting the establishment of units for 
manufacture of the products; pro moting co -operative organization among producers of husks, 
coir fiber, coir yarn and manufactures of coir products; ensuring remunerative returns to

Covid Pandemic and MSME Sector 
 
91. The COVID -19 spread very fast to almost all the countries of the world  and on  11th 
March, 2020, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared it as a Pandemic. In India, the first 
COVID-19 case was reported from Kerala on 30th January, 2020, and subsequently the Pandemic 
spread to almost all the States/UTs. In order to contain the spread of COVID -19 Pandemic, the 
Government of India took various steps such as enforcing social distancing norms, self -isolation 
measures, travel ban, border closure and lockdown of the entire country. 
92. The Pandemic has significantly hampered economic activity all across the world. The 
restricted movement due to lockdown had severe effect on all the sectors of the economy 
especially on the MSMEs  in India . Most of them did not have the capacity to deal with 
something so unexpected and unprecedented. Consequently MSMEs, which rely m ostly on the 
cash availability and informal employment , had to face problems such as sudden dip in or ders 
and cash flows, uncertainty in demand, labour related issues , supply chain disruption etc. 
Particularly the Micro E enterprises that comprised the majority of MSME s suffered massive 
losses due to the lockdowns because they had to run their businesses with only limited resources. 

36 
 
A large number of MSMEs comprising manufacturing and service/retail firms had to shut down 
their business es during nationwide lockdowns due to the disruptions in the supply chain as 
procurement of raw materials at affordable rates became very difficult.  
 
Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyaan 
93. Taking cognizance of the gravity of the situation, the Government announced a series of 
measures under the Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyaan  for ameliorating the MSME s. The 
announcements were focused on various important aspects such as availability of credit, demand 
generation, grievance redressal and handholding of MSMEs etc. The steps inter-alia includes: 
 
(i) The Government has notified composite criteria of classification of MSMEs based on 
Investment in plant & machinery or equipment and Turnover of MSMEs as structural 
change to facilitate both existing as well as new entrepreneurs.  
 
(ii) Earlier process of filing  of Udyog Aaadhar  Memorandum has been replaced by 
Udyam Registration  on a Portal developed by the Ministry of MSME, which  is 
expected to bring about many benefits for the MSMEs to grow in size.  
 
(iii) Financial support to the stressed MSMEs with infusion of Rs. 20,000 crore equity 
support through Subordinate Debt which is likely to benefit more than 2 lakh 
MSMEs. 
 
(iv) Fund of Funds created to infuse equity worth Rs.50,  000 crore in the MSME Sector.  
A Rs.10, 000 crore Corpus Fund to be set up which  would provide equity funding to 
growth potential and viable MSMEs. 
 
(v) Regarding e nsuring timely payment to the MSMEs, the Government of India and 
CPSEs have to clear all receivables of MSMEs within 45 days under the Public 
Procurement Policy which will ease  the liquidity problem of MSMEs.  Besides, 
initiatives have been taken for monitoring settlement of dues of MSMEs by larger 
units (Public and Private) through online SAMADHAN and SAMBANDH Portals. 
 
(vi) Rs. 3 lakh crore collateral free automatic loans for business, including MSMEs. 
 
(vii) Global tender to be disallowed in Government procurement Tenders up  to Rs 200 
crores which will provide more market opportunities to domestic entities.

24thJune, 2020. As on 03.02.2021, a total number of 34 Banks have registered as Member

30.84 crore. The objective of the scheme is to provide personal loan through banks to the 
promoters of stressed MSMEs for infusion as equity/quasi equity in the business and provides 
Sub-Debt support in respect of restructuring of MSMEs. The salient features of the Scheme 
are as under: 
(i)   it provides for Rs. 20.000 crore as subordinate debt for Stressed MSMEs. 
(ii) MSME entrepreneurs of such stressed units find it difficult to bring in this additional 
equity and that in turn severely constrains the survival of these units. 

38

brink of becoming NPA. 
(iv)  Promoter(s) of the MSMEs will be given credit equal to 15% of their stake (equity plus 
debt) or Rs. 75 lakh whichever is lower, Promoter(s) in turn will infuse this amount in the 
MSME unit as equity and thereby enhance the liquidity and maintain debt-equity ratio. 
(v)  90% guarantee coverage for this sub-debt will be given under the scheme and 10% would 
come from the concerned Promoters. 
(vi)  There will be a moratorium of 7 years on payment of principal whereas maximum tenure 
for repayment will be 10 years. 
(vii)  Till date, 34 Banks including all PSU Banks have come on-board by signing MoU with 
CGTMSE for becoming the Member Lending Institution (MLI) of the Scheme.

handholding of MSMEs. It is a unified, empowered, robust, and a technology driven platform 
designed for helping and promoting the MSMEs with the following basic objectives: 

39 
 
● To help the MSMEs in th e present  situation in terms of finance, raw materials, labour, 
permissions etc. 
● To help the MSMEs capture new opportunities including manufacturing of medical items 
& accessories. 
● To identify the sparks, i.e., the bright MSMEs who can withstand at present and become 
national and international champions. 
 
101. The Ministry has setup a Central Control Room in Delhi and 68 State Control Rooms in 
different States for expeditious redressal of issues faced by MSMEs.  Besides, 16 Ministries/ 
Departments and 24 State Governments, 54 Banks/Financial Institutions/Regional Rural Banks 
including 19 Private Sector Banks, have already been on -boarded on the portal to address the 
queries related to Credit in a fast track manner. 52 CPSEs have appointed their respective nodal 
officer for this portal to resolve the queries on fast track mode. Till 31 st January, 2021, a total 
number of 27, 237 grievances were received and 98.33 % i.e. 26,783 has been replied. 
102. Further, various other steps such as (i) Global Market Intelligence System (G.M.I.S) to 
provide actionable market intelligence to MSMEs has been developed and initiated; (ii) MSME -
Development Institutes (DIs) are working closely with Industry Associations and providing 
hand-holding support for bank loans, Udyam registration, e -passes, and GST etc.; (iii) MSME -
DIs are working with State Governments in helping the MSME units for procuring raw materials 
for manufacturing of masks, PPE kits, etc. and; (iv) the rate of interest under “Raw Material 
Assistance Scheme (RMA) against Bank Guarantee” has been reduced by 1.50% per annum 
w.e.f. 1stJune, 2020 and again by 0.50% per annum on 1 st October, 2020 to provide cheaper 
financial assistance to MSME units has been t aken by the Ministry for development of MSME 
Sector. 
103. The Committee notes that Ministry has launched CHAMPIONS Portal for 
grievance redressal of MSME units but many small units are not aware about this 
portal and its functions. The Committee recommends  that adequate steps should be 
taken by the Ministry to create awareness about this portal and more budgetary 
allocations be made for publicity purposes. The use of the Portal may be made as 
simple as possible and also the portal should have an option for Hindi language as 
well as the Regional languages for ease of understanding. 

40 
 
104. As a consequence of COVID -19 Pandemic and subsequent lockdowns, numerous 
MSMEs became stressed and could not sustain their businesses due to u navailability of 
working capital, raw material and manpower. Accordingly the CGSSD Scheme has been 
designed to infuse capital in the form of subordinate debt to the MSMEs, which have either 
become NPA or are on the verge of becoming NPA,  to help them incre ase their liquidity. 
The Committee is of the view that the CGSSD Scheme has the capability of providing much 
desired liquidity to the MSMEs who are desperately in need of capital to sustain their 
business. The Committee therefore, recommends that all the p rocedures and technicalities 
for availing the benefits of the Scheme should be simplified;  irreducible minimum interest 
should be charged; repayment tenure of the loan should be kept at the maximum and; a 
friendly and favourable approach should be adopted  by the banks to help revive the 
MSMEs. 
 Make in India

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE – AT A GLANCE 
 
1. The Committee hopes that the new classification of MSMEs would bring about 
positive changes in the MSME Sector. The Committee therefore, recommends that a study 
needs to be conducted to know the exact impact of COVID -19 Pandemic on the MSME 
Sector and to ascertain what benefits have accrued to the MSME Sector by change of 
criteria for classification of MSMEs and introduction of various Schemes. The Committee 
may also be apprised about the findings of the study for perusal. 
                   (Para 3) 
 
2. The Committee reiterates its recommendation contained in its 297 th Report that the 
growth of MSMEs is concentrated mostly in a few States only which induces the people to 
migrate to those areas  in search of employment and livelihood. Therefore, the Ministry 
should work in the direction of removing all the existing geographical imbalances and 
ensure that equitable presence of MSMEs is there in all the States so that there is 
horizontal industrialization and adequate employment generation to tide over the situation 
created particularly due to COVID-19 Pandemic.  
                   (Para 4) 
 
3. The Committee observes that the allocations of the Ministry were either reduced or 
enhanced at the R.E. stage, but the actual expenditure incurred most of the time is less than 
the Revised Estimate. The Committee is therefore, of the opinion that proper es timation 
should be done by the Ministry beforehand to ensure that budget is utilized optimally as 
far as possible. The Ministry should also monitor the output of its various Schemes, 
including individual components so that the output targets are achieved timely.   
(Para 11) 
 
4. The Budget Estimate for FY 2021-22 is Rs. 15699.65 crore, which seems a significant 
increase vis-à-vis FY 2020-21. However, out of this amount an allocation of Rs. 10,000 crore 
has been earmarked for the Guaranteed Emergency Credit L ine Scheme (GECL) and in 
effect Rs. 5699.65 crore is the actual allocation, which is a reduction from the BE of FY 
202021. The Committee is worried that in absence of adequate funds how the Ministry is 
planning to implement its various schemes effectively in the present scenario of COVID -19 
Pandemic when MSME Sector is starved of funds. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry may ask for an enhanced allocation at the RE Stage for proper 
implementation of its flagship Schemes and strengthening of the MSME Sector.   
(Para 12) 
 
5. The Committee is also of the opinion that the details of the action plan regarding the 
utilization of funds allocated under GECL Scheme should be worked out and furnished to 
the Committee for perusal. 
(Para 13) 
 
6. The Committee observes that the Ministry could utilize only 66% of the RE for the 
FY 2020-21 (up to January, 2021), which is a cause of concern. However, the Ministry cited 
COVID-19 Pandemic as the main reason for the underutilization of allocated funds. On th e 

43 
 
other hand, the Committee is of the opinion that the budget utilization should have been 
more because of the demand created due to COVID -19 Pandemic in the MSME Sector.  
The Committee is of the opinion that MSME Sector presently is in desperate need of fu nds. 
Therefore, the Ministry must ensure that the allocated budget is utilized optimally so that 
MSME Sector may thrive. 
(Para 15) 
 
7. The Committee notes that up to the end of 3 rd quarter of FY 2020 -21, the Ministry 
could utilize only 54% of the actual budget allocation i.e. Rs. 5664.22 crore. The Committee 
is constrained to note the underutilization of allocated funds and  would like to know the 
reasons for continuously projecting inflated demands and thereafter underutilizing the 
funds. The Committee therefore, recommends that proper assessment and planning should 
be made beforehand in respect of utilization of funds quarter -wise so that there is no rush 
to spend more in the last quarters of the year. 
(Para 17) 
 
8. The Committee is of the view that KVIC should concentrate more on its technology 
improvement and products upgradation aspect in this age of stiff competition with big 
market players. The Committee, therefore, recommends that latest training programmes 
by experienced and experts having expertise  in the field should be imparted to the artisans 
through its network of training institutions for product design and quality improvement in 
order to promote export of Khadi products. Further, the Committee recommends that the 
process of revamping and reori entation of KVIs should also be done wherever required so 
that it helps in productivity development of Khadi and Village Industries. 
(Para 23) 
 
9. The Committee raised concern over difference in BE i.e. Rs. 905 crore for FY 2021 -
22 vis-à-vis BE for FY 2020 -21 i.e. Rs. 1525 crore for Khadi Sector as this being an 
important sector which generates large scale employment for rural people. The Committee 
recommends that considering the importance of Khadi Sector and its employment 
generating potential, an increased budget allocation should be asked for at RE stage by the 
Ministry.  
(Para 24) 
 
10. Recently Khadi Prakritik Paint  has been developed and launched by Khadi and Village 
Industries Commission. The paint is said to be cow dung based, eco -friendly, non-toxic product 
with anti -fungal, anti -bacterial properties. It is claimed that the paint is cost -effective and 
odorless and has been certified by Bureau of Indian Standards. The Committee appreciates the 
efforts made by the KVIC and recommends tha t such type of initiatives and innovations 
take place regularly with the combination of innovative ideas and latest technology. The  
Committee therefore, recommends that adequate funds should be allocated for R&D and 
Technology related support facilities in order to improve the quality of Khadi products vis-
a-vis international products. 
(Para 25) 
 

44 
 
11. The Committee appreciates the effort made by the Ministr y in respect of creating e -
market linkages for strengthening the MSME Sector and recommends that the Ministry 
should analyze the marketing system of MSMEs of developed countries and their system of 
newer technology adoption for their development and adopt the best practices followed 
internationally for advancement and development of indigenous MSMEs.  
(Para 28) 
 
12. The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Ministry in providing financial 
help to Khadi artisans during Covid Pandemic through Artisan Welfare Fund Trust.  The 
Committee recommends that some kind of contingent fund or financial provision should be 
put in place by the Ministry keeping in view the welfare of the artisans associated with 
MSME Sector for the unforeseen situations like Covid P andemic as a social security 
measure so that some kind of monetary help can be provided to artisans in times of distress 
in future.  
(Para 31) 
 
13. PMEGP is one of the flagship Schemes of the Ministry of MSME which is capable of 
generating large-scale employment for youth of the country, particularly during the Covid 
Pandemic. The Committee however finds that an amount Rs. 2000 crore has been allocate d 
for the Scheme for FY 2021 -2022 vis-à-vis allocation of Rs. 2500 crores during 2020 -2021. 
The Committee recommends that more allocations should be demanded by the Ministry at 
the RE stage for effective implementation of the Scheme. 
(Para 37) 
 
14. The Com mittee is concerned to note that out of the total number of applications 
received under the Scheme, around 76% were forwarded to the banks, only 16% of the 
applications got sanctioned by the banks and a meager 10% of applications got 
disbursements by the b anks. Since PMEGP Scheme is one of the flagship Schemes of the 
Ministry, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should look into the matter and 
take steps for removing the hindrances and simplifying the procedures with minimal 
formalities and technical ities so as to ensure that  off take of loan under the scheme is 
improved. 
(Para 38) 
 
15. The Committee notes that there is huge difference between Margin Money 
allocation and Margin Money utilization in NER.  Also the number of units assisted are 
very few. Employment generation is also negligible. The Committee recommends that more 
clusters/LBIs/TBIs should be set up by the Ministry in NER to overcome the problems of 
unemployment, poverty, drudgery and migration. The Committee also recommends that 
massive awareness programmes should also be organized by the Ministry in NER to create 
awareness a mong people in NER regarding various beneficial programmes/schemes 
implemented by the Ministry.  
(Para 39) 
 
16. During the course of discussion on the DFG (2021 -2022), the Committee observes 
that the constraints faced by KVIC/KVIB are due to procedural del ays, inadequate 

45 
 
technology up -gradation, underutilization of funds etc. Despite providing technical 
guidance to the units in KVI, the problems of the units remain inadequately addressed, as a 
result there is suboptimal functioning of institutions/units and  high drop outs among new 
entrants and low employment generation.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
KVIC should come forward with a more pragmatic approach in coordination with all the 
stakeholders. Proper planning, monitoring and implementation of each scheme are 
required to meet the primary objective of employ ment generation, particularly to counter 
COVID-19 Pandemic like situations in future.  
(Para 41) 
 
17. The Committee is of the view that the youths in urban as well as rural areas are not 
inclined to work in KVI Sector due to low wages and the hardships inv olved in it.  
Therefore, the Committee desires that the economic empowerment of the poor artisans can 
be enhanced by allowing the potential artisans (spinners and weavers) to work with the 
private Designer Houses of national and international reputation wit hout the approval of 
KVIC so that they could earn more wages from them directly.  
(Para 42) 
 
18. The Committee observes that Schemes like ISEC, PMEGP etc. of the Ministry are 
not working satisfactorily in North Eastern Region and has a very negligible pres ence in 
the NER.  Even the implementation of the Strengthening of Infrastructure of Existing 
Weak Khadi Institution Scheme is not encouraging. The Committee recommends that 
initiatives should be taken by the Ministry for revival of weak Khadi Institutions with the 
help of State Governments in the NER, which has a vigorous craft tradition and manifests 
itself in its various products from cane and bamboo handicrafts to metalwork and gorgeous 
textiles. 
(Para 43) 
 
19. The Committee observes that the ISEC issued  and bank finance provided to the 
Institutions is not very encouraging, mainly due to the existence of problems like lack of 
awareness among the people or some kind of procedural hassles. The Committee therefore, 
recommends that adequate steps should be ta ken by the Ministry to organize awareness 
programs and utilise social media to popularize the Scheme. To increase the off take, the 
procedures may be simplified, formalities may be kept at minimum, and banks may be 
educated about the Scheme and advised to adopt friendly and favourable approach while 
considering the applications and claims. 
(Para 48) 
 
20. The Committee observes that the ISEC issued and the amount disbursed to the 
Khadi Institutions in the North Eastern Regions is not very encouraging. The Co mmittee 
therefore, recommends that reasons responsible for underperformance of the Scheme 
should be ascertained and informed to the Committee for perusal.  Remedial measures 
should also be taken by the Ministry for improving the off take of the Scheme in N ER 
which is lagging behind in comparison to other states of the country. 
(Para 49) 
 

46 
 
21. The Committee notes that the BE for SFURTI Scheme for FY 2020-21 i.e. Rs. 464.85 
crore was reduced at the RE Stage to Rs. 300 crore and the Actual Expenditure was only 
Rs. 192.54 crores till 31 st January, 2021. The Committee also notes that against a projected 
Budget Estimate of Rs. 500 crore for the SFRUTI Scheme for FY 2021 -2022, an allocation 
of only Rs. 170 crore has been made. The Committee expresses its concern ove r the low 
utilization pattern and reduction in allocations for an important Scheme of the Ministry, 
which is capable of generating employment in a large scale in the rural areas for the 
artisans, particularly during the Covid Pandemic. The Committee recomm ends that a 
holistic evaluation study of the Scheme may be conducted and based on the said study more 
allocations should be projected by the Ministry at the RE Stage for effective 
implementation of SFURTI Scheme for benefit of the traditional artisans. 
(Para 53) 
 
22. The Committee is constrained to note that out of 371 clusters which have been 
approved, only 82 clusters are operational so far. The Committee recommends that the 
process of setting up of SFURTI clusters should be expedited; targets should be set and 
ensure that the approved clusters are completed and become operational within the 
stipulated timeframe for benefit of artisans.   
(Para 54) 
 
23. The Committee was apprised by the Ministry that besides 219 Districts, 56 
Aspirational Districts have also been covered under SFURTI. The Committee recommends 
that more attention should be paid to target more and more Aspirational Districts across 
the country as this can immensely improve the socio-economic conditions of the inhabitants 
in those districts and improve the human development index. The Ministry may coordinate 
with the state governments and with concerted efforts desired results may be achieved.  
(Para 55) 
 
24. During the Covid Pandemic induced lockdowns, scores of migrant workers were 
forced to return to their native places and had to stay back for months without any 
livelihood/ employment.  SFURTI is one such Scheme which has the potential to generate 
employment in rural areas with less investment for the artisans. The Committee 
recommends that Ministry should endeavour to set up more SFURTI clusters and ensure 
that each and every district of the country has SFURTI clusters on the lines of one -district 
one-product to solve the problem of unemployment in rural areas.   
(Para 56) 
 
25. The Committee observes that one of the most important objectives of the 
implementation of various Schemes under Coir Board is the creation of employment 
especially in rural areas of the country.  For this purpose, Coir Board is providing training 
on various aspects of production and development of new/innovative products. The 
Committee recommends that Ministry should make these training courses popular through 
various social publicity mediums available so that large number of people especially from 
younger generation may get attracted to such training courses which will culminate in 
fruitful employment. 
(Para 61) 

47 
 
26. The Committee notes that export performance of coir and coir products during 
2020-21 is not encouraging, which may be due to Covid Pandemic and consequent 
lockdowns. The Committee recommends that necessary remedial measures may be taken 
by the Coir Board for restoring the export performance as the impact of  Covid is 
improving gradually. Further, the Committee recommends that high targets for exports 
should be set and endeavour should be made to achieve those targets by effective planning 
and execution. Latest technology and techniques should be adopted for m aking coir 
products more competitive to meet the international standards.  
(Para 62) 
 
27. The Committee observes that the Skill Development Programmes organised 
especially in respect of the ‘Physically Handicapped’ Category is not up to the mark. The 
Committee accordingly recommends that more Skill Development Programmes may be 
organized among various categories of people for improving their skills for gainful 
employment in the coir sector. Online training sessions may also be organized as per 
feasibility and practicality. 
(Para 63) 
 
28. The Committee notes that an allocation of Rs. 100 crore was made in BE for Solar 
Charkha Mission for FY 2020 -21 but at the RE Stage it got only Rs. 0.04 crore. Further, 
for FY 2021-22, an allocation of Rs. 5.04 crore has been made at BE Stage. The Committee 
recommends that more budgetary allocations should be made for such a good and eco 
friendly scheme capable of providing employment in rural areas and accordingly, t he 
Ministry should project for more allocations at RE St age for setting up of more Solar 
Charkha Clusters across the country. Besides, the Ministry should provide timely 
interventions so that the Solar Charkha Clusters so set up are operationalized in an 
expeditious manner. 
(Para 65) 
 
29. The Committee desires that the data regarding the CLCS Component may also be 
provided for its perusal thereof. Besides, Technology Upgradation is need of the hour as 
technology is evolving and changing at a fast pace day by day. Moreover technology 
upgradation for MSME Sector i s equally important to keep them competitive in the 
domestic as well as international market. The Committee recommends that some sort of 
international collaboration for technology sharing/transfer should be undertaken for all 
round development of indigenou s MSMEs. Besides, more budgetary allocations should be 
made for adoption of latest and cutting edge technology in view of the changing market 
scenarios.   
(Para 69) 
 
30. The Committee is of the view that for Technology Upgradation, research and 
development are very important for all round development of MSME Sector. The 
Committee therefore, recommends that more funds should be allocated, which is only Rs. 
330.31 crores in the BE for FY 2021-2022 vis-à-vis Rs. 1095.67 crores allocated at RE stage 
in FY 2020-2021, for Technology Upgradation and R&D purposes for strengthening of the 
MSMEs.   

48 
 
(Para 70) 
 
31. During the lockdown periods the availability of raw material was disrup ted which 
affected the operations of MSMEs adversely. Further, the prices of raw material have risen 
exorbitantly in the recent times which have significantly affected the businesses of the 
MSMEs and their profits have significantly decreased. In this give n scenario, NSIC can 
play a significant role by coordinating with the respective Ministries to ensure unhindered 
supply of raw material to MSMEs and also provided support and interventions to the 
MSMEs in the export of their products. The Committee expresses its satisfaction that NSIC 
performed well since II Quarter and facilitated the MSMEs to the tune of Rs. 1234.91 
crores. The Committee is however, of the view that the Ministry should also explore other 
possibilities for raw material supply to MSMEs inst ead of solely depending on NSIC to 
meet the raw material requirements of MSMEs. 
(Para 73) 
 
32. The Committee recommends that a robust procurement system should be evolved 
which could ensure unhindered and timely supply of raw materials to MSMEs at 
reasonable price. The Committee recommends that required steps should be taken to keep 
the prices of raw material reasonable, including giving some sort of subsidy, so that 
MSMEs can run their businesses smoothly.  
(Para 74) 
 
33. The Committee desired that delay in payments by CPSEs and Government 
Departments affects MSMEs adversely as they need cash flow to run their businesses. The 
Committee however, recommends that delayed payments of MSMEs from CPSEs be 
monitored through the SA MBANDH and SAMADHAAN Portals regularly and the 
pending payments of MSMEs may be cleared by CPSEs and other Government agencies at 
the earliest for strengthening the liquidity of MSMEs. 
(Para 78) 
 
34. The Committee notes that TReDS is a new initiative by th e Ministry of MSME for 
resolving the problem of delayed payments to MSMEs by CPSEs/Government Agencies. 
Making penal provision of 1% per month for erring buyers will definitely prove to be a 
deterrent for defaulting buyers. The Committee expects that the p enal provision is 
enforced in letter and spirit. The Committee hopes that TReDS will able to solve the 
problem of delayed payments and improve the liquidity position of the MSMEs. The 
Committee recommends that TReDS should be implemented strictly and monit ored 
regularly and the MSMEs may be exempted from paying charges for on -boarding this 
platform beyond 31st March 2021. 
(Para 79) 
 
35. The Committee observes that NSIC through its Vendor Development Programmes 
sensitize and facilitate MSEs, including SC/ST enterprises, to become qualified vendors to 
public sector enterprises and other Government Departments as per the provision of 25% 
mandatory procurement under Public Procurement Policy. Of this, 4% should be from 
SC/ST MSEs. However, during its visit to Ko lkata, Hyderabad and Mumbai in January, 

49 
 
2020, the Committee found that while the PSUs and Government procurement from MSEs 
has been gradually improving, procurement from SC/ST units is negligible. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that there should be mo re Vendor Development Programmes 
organized to popularize Public Procurement Policy among MSEs especially SC/ST and 
Women entrepreneurs. 
(Para 83) 
 
36. The Committee notes that the pace of expenditure under the NSCST Hub Scheme is 
not at all encouraging and that the allocation of Rs. 150 crore in the BE 2020-2021 has been 
reduced to Rs. 120 crore at the RE Stage. Further, the allocation for FY 2021 -2022 has also 
been kept at Rs. 120 crore at the BE Stage. The Committee fails to understand the reasons 
for such slow pace of expending in respect of such an important Scheme, which has been 
specially formulated for the marginalized section of the society. The C ommittee 
recommends that the Ministry should take adequate steps to speed up the spending 
process, so that allocated amount gets utilized to the optimum.  
(Para 84) 
 
37. The Committee observes that under National SC/ST Hub, the Actual Expenditure 
has always been less than the BE. The Committee is concerned about the under -utilization 
of allocated funds meant for the marginalized communities of the society. The Committee 
recommends that Ministry should endeavor to improve the situation by ensuring that the 
budget earmarked for SC/ST Hub Scheme is utilized fully for the benefit of the 
communities. Creating awareness among SC/ST entrepreneurs, ground level support and 
handholding of SC/ST entrepreneurs may work well in improving the performance of this 
scheme. Underutilization of funds is a serious cause of concern for the Committee; 
therefore, Ministry is advised to ensure full utilization of funds. 
(Para 85) 
 
38. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should create an All India Database 
of SC/ST entrepreneurs’ locations and vocations and share the same with CPSEs so that 
CPSEs can locate SC/ST units easily for availing their services. Also, the SC/ST Hub 
should run NSQF compliant skill development programmes for SC/ST technicians who 
could take contract jobs and services that CPSEs outsource. 
(Para 86) 
 
39. The trend under Public Procurement Policy has not been encouraging over the 
years. The Committee therefore, recommends that the trend should be reversed and 
adequate steps should be taken by the Ministry to ensure fair participation of SC/ST MSEs 
in Public Procurement Policy.  The Committee also recommends that more special VDPs 
should be organized for SC/ST entrepreneurs for improving their participation in Public 
Procurement Policy. The Ministry  should also adopt handholding approach while 
promoting SC/ST entrepreneurs.   
(Para 87)

satisfactorily in North Eastern Region and has a very negligible presence in these areas.

people of NER through its various schemes with the help of State Governments 
particularly potential women and SC/ST entrepreneurs be encouraged to participate in the 
growth process. 
(Para 88)

convenient and cheaper for MSMEs and they should be provided some sort of subsidy for 
availing such testing facilities. It is also required that a mechanism should be developed so

issued from various global testing centres, which are acceptable in respective 
countries/regions.

redressal of MSME units but many small units are not aware about this portal and its

REPORT 
The Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) are rightly hailed as „the temples of modern India.‟ 
They were conceived to be a critical component of our mixed economy and were put into 
operation for transforming the independent India into a modern and industrially advanced nation. 
Primacy given to the CPSEs arose out of the fact that the private enterprises were not adequately 
equipped to undertake the mammoth task of creating infrastructure and other facilities which 
were indispensable for nation -building. The contribution of PSEs towards the growth of Indian 
economy through measures such as generation of income, capital formation, generation of 
employment, development of infrastructure facilities, building a strong industrial base, export 
promotion and impor t substitution, contribution to central exchequer, removal of regional 
disparities, checking concentration of income & wealth etc. is really commendable. 
 The Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) in India 
2. The Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSE s) comprise enterprises established by the 
Government of India (GOI) as Government companies under Section 617 of the Companies Act, 
and wherein the equity holding of the GOI is more than 50 per cent. It also includes statutory 
corporations constituted und er specific statutes of the Parliament. The CPSEs do not, however, 
include departmental undertakings, banking institutions and enterprises where equity holding of 
the GOI is 50% or less.  
3. The number of CPSEs has increased from 5 during the first five ye ar plan to 366 as on 
31.3.2020. The cumulative investment (paid up capital plus long term loans), which was Rs. 29 
crore in 5 enterprises as on 31.03.1951, has gone up to Rs.  20.62 lakh crore in 366 CPSEs.  Out 
of these 366 CPSEs, 256 are in Operation, 96 CPSEs have yet to commence business and 14 are 
under liquidation or approved for closure. Out of 256 operating CPSEs as many as 171 CPSEs 
showed profit during 2019 -20, 83 CPSEs incurred losses during the year, and 1 CPSE had no 
profit no loss. The Central Public Sector Enterprises are under the administrative control of 
various Ministries/ Departments and decision with regard to major investments, expansion, 
diversification, joint ventures, modernisation, technology upgradation, etc. are taken by the 
CPSEs in consultation with their respective administrative Ministries/Departments. 
 Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) 
4.      In their 52nd Report, the Estimates Committee of 3rd Lok Sabha (1962 -67) stressed the 
need for setting up a centralized coordinatin g unit, which could also make continuous appraisal 
of the performance of public enterprises. This led to the setting up of the Bureau of Public 
Enterprises (BPE) in 1965 in the Ministry of Finance. Subsequently, as a result of the 
reorganization of the Ministries/Departments of the Union Government in September, 1985, BPE 
was made part of the Ministry of Industry. In May, 1990, BPE was made a full fledged 
Department known as the DPE. Presently, it is part of the Ministry of Heavy Industries & Public 
Enterprises (Mo HI &PE).                            
 

2 
 
5.      The DPE is the nodal department for all the CPSEs and formulates policy pertaining to 
them. It lays down, in particular, policy guidelines on performance improvement and evaluation, 
autonomy and financi al delegation and personnel management in CPSEs. It further collects and 
maintains information in the form of a Public Enterprises Survey on several areas in respect of 
CPSEs.        
6.      In fulfilling its role, the Department coordinates with other Min istries, CPSEs and 
concerned organizations. As per the Allocation of Business Rules of the Government, the 
following subjects have been allocated to the DPE: 
 Coordination of matters of general policy affecting all Public-Sector Enterprises.  
 Residual work relating to erstwhile Bureau of Public Enterprises including Industrial 
Management Pool. 
 Evaluation and monitoring the performance of Public Sector Enterprises, including the 
Memorandum of Understanding mechanism. 
 Matters relating to Permanent Machinery of  Arbitration for the Public -Sector 
Enterprises.  
 Counselling, training and rehabilitation of employees in Central Public Sector 
Undertakings under Voluntary Retirement Scheme. 
 Review of capital projects and expenditure in Central Public Sector Enterprises. 
 Measures aimed at improving performance of Central Public Sector Enterprises and other 
capacity building initiatives of Public Sector Enterprises. 
 Rendering advice relating to revival, restructuring or closure of Public Sector Enterprises 
including the mechanisms therefore. 
 Matters relating to Standing Conference of Public Enterprises. 
 Matters relating to International Center for Public Enterprises. 
 Categorization of Central Public Sector Enterprises including conferring „Ratna‟ status. 
 Survey of Public Enterprises. 
7.      According to the Annual Report of the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public 
Enterprises the Vision and Mission statements of DPE are as follows: 
 Vision 
 “Effective, Profitable and Globally Competitive Central Public Sector Enterprises” 
 Mission 
  “To continuously improve management and performance of CPSEs through Corporate 
Governance, Performance Evaluation, Human Resource Management, Research & Development 
so as to enhance their global competitiveness”

Categorization of CPSEs 
12.  CPSEs are categorized into four schedules  namely „A‟, „B‟, „C‟ & „D‟ based on criteria 
such as quantitative parameters, i.e., Investment, Capital Employed, Net Sales, Profit before Tax, 
Number of employees and units, Capacity Addition, Revenue per employee, Sales/Capital 
Employed, Capacity Utiliz ation, Value added per employee as well as qua litative  parameters, 

4 
 
i.e., National importance, Complexities of the problems being faced by the company, Level of 
technology, Prospects of expansion and diversification and competition from other sectors are t o 
be considered while examining such proposals. In addition, critical/strategic importance of the 
concerned CPSE as well as factors such as Share price, MoU ratings, Ratna status, ISO 
certification are also taken into consideration. 
13.        The present procedure of categorization of CPSEs involves consideration of the 
proposals in the administrative Ministry concerned and the Department of Public Enterprises 
which consults the Public Enterprises Selection Board. The categorization of CPSEs has 
implications mainly for organizational structure and salary of Board level incumbents of the 
concerned CPSE. It also plays a role in grant of autonomy to the Board s of CPSEs under „Ratna‟ 
scheme. A s informed by DPE, at present there are 66 Schedule „A‟, 65 Schedule „B‟, 44 
Schedule „C‟ and 5 Schedule „D‟ CPSEs. The schedule -wise list of CPSEs is given in 
Annexure-I.                                                                                          
   Autonomy of CPSEs 
14.     The endeavor of the Government is t o make Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) 
autonomous board managed companies. Under Articles of Association, the Board of Directors of 
CPSEs enjoys autonomy in respect of recruitment, promotion and other service conditions of 
below board level emplo yees. The Board of Directors of a CPSE exercises delegated powers 
subject to broad policy guidelines issued by Government from time to time. The Government has 
granted enhanced powers to the Boards of the profit -making enterprises under various schemes 
like Maharatna, Navratna and Miniratna by delegating powers in the areas of (i) capital 
expenditure, (ii) investment in joint ventures/subsidiaries, (iii) mergers & acquisitions, (iv) 
human resources management, etc.  
15. The main objective of the Maharatna s cheme which was introduced in 2010 is to 
empower mega CPSEs to expand their operations and emerge as global giants. The Maharatna 
Scheme empowers big sized CPSEs to expand their operations and emerge as global giants.The 
Government had introduced the Navra tna scheme, in 1997, to identify Central Public Sector 
Enterprises (CPSEs) that had comparative advantages and to support them in their drive to 
become global giants.  In October 1997, the Government had decided to grant enhanced 
autonomy and delegation of financial powers to some other profit making companies subject to 
certain eligibility conditions and guidelines to make them efficient and competitive. These 
companies, called Miniratna, are in two categories, namely, Category - I and Category -II. As 
informed by DPE, p resently there are 10 Maharatna CPSEs, 14 Navratna CPSEs and 73 
Miniratna CPSEs (61 Miniratna category-I and 12 Miniratna category-II) (Annexure-II).

issued by the Ministry of Finance (MoF) with regard to rationalization of Schemes, the  Scheme 
for Skill Development/Training programme to executives/employees of State Level Public 
Enterprises (SLPEs) was merged with the Scheme of RDC on Generic issues of Public Sector 
Enterprises (PSEs) during the year 2016-17. 

10 
 
32.    RDC scheme was modified so that activities could be spread round the year and its scope 
was expanded and diversified to include more activities. Some of the features of revised scheme 
are elaborated as under: 
        i.          Thematic studies and consultancies on generic is sues like corporate governance, 
Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) system, professionalization, project management, risk 
management, human resource management, Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) etc. related 
to Public Sector Enterprises are undertaken. I n addition, benchmarking studies on selected 
sectors are also undertaken to enable enterprises to move towards achieving those benchmarks 
and become nationally /internationally competitive. 
      ii.          With objective to gain experience in many ways of learning and to keep engaged 
through learning activities seminars, workshops, conferences, etc. on various generic issues are 
organized. After coming into force of the provisions of Companies Act, 2013 on Corporate 
Social Responsibility (CSR), frequent meets are held. 
    iii.          Under RDC Scheme, MoU is very important instrument towards improving the 
performance of the CPSEs. Some modifications and improvements made in MoU mechanism 
since 2016 -17 include (i) proposed result oriented parameters (ii ) Parameter included for 
monitoring CAPEX contracts/projects running/completed without time/cost overrun (iii) CAPEX 
parameter weightage has been increased; and (iv) Procurement policy issued by Ministry of 
MSME has been given importance. Efforts are being  made for online system based on a single 
window concept for all MoU related matters for all stakeholders. Task force system has been 
dispensed with and now, Inter- Ministerial Committee of MoU has taken place. 
    iv.          DPE supplements the efforts of CPSEs/ SLPEs in improving / upgrading the skills of 
managers / executives / employees through capacity building Skill Development / Training 
Programmes for upgrading the skills and knowledge of their executives. To supplement the 
efforts of SLPEs/CPSEs,  DPE conducts training programmes in collaboration with some of the 
premier management / training institutes IITs, IIMs, ASCI, IIPA etc. This enables wider 
exposure and sharing of experience on pertinent issues. 
      v.          The guidelines on Corporate Governance for CPSEs issued by DPE stipulate training to 
newly inducted Non Official Directors (NODs) in the business model of the company. Besides 
induction training by CPSEs with a view to familiarize with the rules and regulations, business 
module, risk profile etc., DPE also in collaboration with respective CPSEs, from time to time, 
organizes general short term training for NODs, official directors and other Directors on the 
boards of CPSEs on relevant areas including model code of business ethics and  conduct of the 
company. This enriches the board in suggesting the best solution for short/long term viability/ 
profitability of the enterprises. 
    vi.          The objective of International Centre for Promotion of Enterprises (ICPE) Ljubljana, 
Slovenia is to promote and support enterprise development in developing countries in both 
private and public sector. ICPE is an intergovernmental organization. Being a founder member 
of ICPE, India has been taking active part in its activities by way of attending Council/Assembly 
Sessions regularly at the level of Secretary.

MoU System for CPSEs 
64.    The Government of India introduced the MoU system in the year 1986, based on the 
recommendations given by Arjun Sen Gupta Committee Report (1984) . The report 
recommended that the CPSEs should enter agreement with their administrative Ministries for 
five years, with progress to be reviewed annually. The MoU system was given broader thrust by 
the Governments after the announcement of the New Industrial Policy of 1991. 
65.    DPE monitors and evaluates the profitability and efficacy of MoU signing CPSEs 
through their MoU targets & their evaluation to measure the performance of the management of 
the CPSEs on key selected parameters so as to improve the critical performance indicators of the 
organization. 
66.    MoU guidelines are reviewed from time to time based on the feedback received from 
Administrative Ministries/ CPSEs and based on the changes occurred in the Regulations. 
67. Some of the main points  of the latest MoU Guideline issued by DPE on 17th January, 
2019 are as under:- 
1. Memorandum of Understanding: MoU is a negotiated agreement and contract between 
the Administrative Ministry/Department/ Holding CPSEs i.e. majority shareholder and the 
Management of the Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSE) on selected parameters having 
targets decided normally before the start of a new financial year and results evaluated af ter the 

20 
 
end of the year to measure  the performance. MoU system involves target set ting in financial and 
non- financial areas and performance evaluation of those targets. 
2. Purpose of MoU:  The purpose of the MoU is to measure the performance of the 
management of the CPSEs on key selected parameters against the targets agreed upon so as to 
improve the critical performance indicators of the organisation. 
3. Scope: All CPSEs (Holding as well as Subsidiaries) are required to sign MoUs. The 
Holding companies will signMoUs with their administrative Ministries/ Departments, while the 
Subsidiary companies will sign MoUs with their respective Holding companies. 
 
4. Exemption from MoU:The following CPSEs are exempted from MoU system: 
 
i.     CPSEs under liquidation where Liquidator has already been appointed. Administrative 
Ministry would provide the list of such CPSEs. 
ii.       CPSEs which are not in operation or having no employees or on any other ground on 
the recommendation of administrative Ministry with approval of InterMinisterial 
Committee or High Powered Committee. 
5.     Parameters: CPSEs work in various sectors under different conditions. In view of this, the 
following guidelines are laid down:- 
5.1    For 50% weightage, t here would be uniform parameters for measuring financial 
performances such as revenue from operations, operating profi t and return on investment (e.g. 
ratio of PAT/Net -worth). This would be applicable to all CPSEs, except CPSEs which are 
dependent on government grant or performing functions of distribution of grant etc. e.g. 
Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Coun cil (BIRAC). Hence, 3 financial parameters 
have been prescribed for all CPSEs with total weightage of 50% except for CPSEs like BIRAC. 
5.2    For the remaining 50% weightage, a menu of parameters has been suggested for selection 
depending on the sector in which the CPSE is operating. Separate Format has been given for 
Finance Sector and another Format for the remaining operating CPSEs. The parameters most 
appropriate and relevant for measuring performance shall be suggested by the Pre -Negotiation 
Committee (PNC) to the Inter -Ministerial Committee (IMC). In all the cases IMC shall take 
appropriate decision on the suggestions made by PNC. 
5.3    Chairman, IMC is authorised to modify the parameters or weightages of parameters in 
sector specific cases, if justified. 
6. High Powered Committee (HPC) : The High -Powered Committee (HPC) is the Apex 
body under MoU system for laying policy guidelines, approval of the benchmarks and indices 
recommended by IMC.   
7. Pre-negotiation Committee (PNC):  The role of the Pre -negotiation Committee (earlier 
known as Standing Committee on MoU) would be to assist IMC in determining the most 
appropriate and relevant parameters for measuring improvement in performance and for fixing 
targets. Meetings of the Pre -negotiation Committee wou ld be held in each case before the 
meetings of IMC to look at the trends, discuss, negotiate and recommend MoU parameters and 

21 
 
targets. The Pre -negotiation committee comprises Adviser (MoU), DPE, concerned Joint 
Secretary/Adviser of Administrative Ministry, concerned Adviser (NITI Aayog), Director (MoU) 
and representative from Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation (MoSPI). 
8. Inter-Ministerial Committee (IMC) : MoU targets are decided by the IMC. Inter -
Ministerial Committee on MoU consists of Secr etary, DPE as Chairman, Secretary of concerned 
administrative Ministry/Department or his representative not below the rank of Joint Secretary 
(Member), Secretary, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation or his representative 
not below the rank of Joint Secretary (Member), Additional Secretary, NITI Aayog or his 
representative (Member). Secretary, DPE may co -opt any officer who is a finance expert in case 
the need is felt. 
9. Time-lines for submission of MoU:  The draft MoU with all documents/ Ann exures 
should be submitted to administrative Ministry/ Department in respect of all CPSEs and their 
subsidiaries by 21st November of each year for the forthcoming year. The draft MoU after the 
approval of administrative Ministry/ Department should be sent to DPE by 15th December of 
each year for the forthcoming year with all documents/Annexures. Administrative Ministry/ 
Department would ensure that the targets are realistic, growth -oriented, aspirational and 
consistent with the latest Annual Plan, Budget and Corporate Plan of the CPSEs. 
10.   MoU Signing Process :MoU based on the parameters, targets and weightage 
recommended by IMC without any deviation shall be signed between CMD/ MD of CPSE and 
Secretary of administrative Ministry/ Department in case of holding/ independent CPSEs and 
between CEO/ MD of subsidiary company and CMD/ MD of holding CPSE in case of subsidiary 
by 31st March (i.e. before start of financial year in respect of which targets are fixed) or within 
21 days from issue of IMC meeting minutes, whichever is later. In case, deviation is detected, 
IMC minutes would prevail. 
11.   MoU Evaluation: Evaluation of MoU of the CPSE is done after the end of the year on 
the basis of actual achievements vis -à-vis the MoU targets. CPSEs (Holding as well a s 
Subsidiaries) are required to submit performance evaluation reports on the basis of audited 
accounts to Department of Public Enterprises after approval of the Board of CPSE and through 
the administrative Ministries/Departments on or before 30th September  (in respect of 
immediately preceding year) or any other date communicated by DPE. Figures and information 
in the MoU achievement which are not verifiable from audited accounts would be relied on the 
basis of certification by way of resolution of the Board given separately for each parameter.

Revival/ Restructuring/ Closure and Disinvestment of CPSEs 
 
72. The Committee wanted to know the reasons for the l osses/ sickness in CPSEs. The 
Department in their written submission informed that some common problems for sickness in 
CPSEs include old and obsolete   plant  and machinery, outdated technology, low capacity 
utilization, low productivity, poor debt –equity structure, excess manpower, weak marketing 
strategies, stiff competition, lack of business plans, dependence on government orders, heavy 
interest burden, high input cost, resource crunch, etc. Further with privatization, liberalization 
and opening up of the economy, those CPSEs which did not change along with the fast -changing 
times lost ground to private companies and turned loss making and sick.  
 
73. The Committee hopes that the I nter Ministerial consultative process, together with 
DPE's role as a mentor  and guide would facilitate the incipient sick and weak CPSEs into 
taking mid -term course , corrections so that they are saved from entering into the 'sick' 
bandwagon and likewise the 'weak' CPSEs would be able to nurse t hemselves back into 
good financial health.  
 
74. The Government has taken many steps to make the mechanism and process for revival/ 
restructuring of CPSE time bound, comprehensive, performance driven and efficient.  The 
Government has decided to remove multiple layers in the decision making p rocess to ensure 
timely revival/ restructuring of sick CPSEs. It has been decided that revival/restructuring of sick/ 
incipient sick CPSEs is to be merit based taking into account strategic, national and business 
concerns of the CPSE. 
 
75. The DPE had on 2 9th October, 2015 laid down guidelines for streamlining the 
mechanism for restructuring/ revival or closure of sick or incipient sick CPSEs and weak CPSEs 
which were revised on 07th September 2016. Further, on 14th June 2018, DPE again issued 
revised guidelines on „time bound closure   of  sick/loss making CPSEs and disposal of movable 
and immovable assets. These replace the earlier guidelines issued by DPE on this subject. 
 
76. The guidelines are intended to expeditiously complete the procedures for closure  of 
CPSEs and lay down responsibilities   of the concerned Ministries/ Departments/ CPSE, etc., 
including the support required to be extended by nodal Departments/ Organizations like, 
Ministry of Finance, NITI Aayog, etc. The revised guidelines prescribe a matrix of timelines for 
step by step process to be completed in respect of a CPSE under closure and about disposal of its 
assets. The guidelines on time bound closure of sick/ loss making CPSEs uniformly provide for 
payment of VRS/VSS at 2007 notional pay scale to employees of CPSEs under closure 
irrespective of the existing pay scales of the company.

Disinvestment 
80. The Committee is aware of the fact  that the Finance Minister has set a Disinvestment 
target of Rs.1.75 lakh crores  for the current financial year . The FM  unveiled the Public Sector 
Enterprises ( PSE) Policy for Atmanirbhar Bharat and announced that barring four strategic 
sectors, Public Sector Enterprises in other sectors will be divested.  The following sectors are 
specified as strategic sectors:- 
 
(i) Atomic Energy, Space and Defence; 
(ii) Transport and Telecommunication; 
(iii) Power, Petroleum, coal and other miners; and 
(iv) Banking, Insurance and Financial Services.  
81. The Committee sought the details of   the role of DPE in operationalising and achieving  
the disinvestment targets set for the year 2021 -22. The DPE informed that Department of 
Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) is the nodal Department for the New Public 
Sector Enterprises Policy on CPSEs, disinvestment and asset monetization of C PSEs and their 
implementation. The subject matter does not come under the purview of DPE. DIPAM on 04 th 
February, 2021 has issued operational modalities of the New Public Sector Enterprises policy. 
82. Besides, the Secretary in his deposition before the Co mmittee, while making presentation 
on the Demands for Grants 2021 -22, had stated that in order to get a better return on the 
investments of a CPSE, the governm ent sometimes has to go for  disinvestment which exposes 
the company to a wider competition in the market. Such competition provides the Company, a 

25 
 
 platform for a turnaround for the better. Accordingly, some CPSEs that are even profit making 
are being disinvested, while others that are loss making, but cater to strategic sector may not be 
disinvested. 
83. The Committee is of the view that all efforts should be made to infuse the requisite 
capital into the CPSEs, so as to enable them to stand shoulder to shoulder with the private 
entities and offer stiff competition to them. The Committee feels that CPS Es had always 
played a vital role in unbundling privitisation sin ce a long time and thus deserve  the much 
needed support. 
84. The Committee's view is that CPSEs are the backbone of the economy and there 
should be no stone left unturned to strengthen the CP SEs that are profit making and 
adding their contribution to the nation economic kitty.  The Committee also desires that it 
be apprised of the reasons as to why the reviving and restructuring mechanisms failed to 
have any positive effect on the loss making CPSEs.  
85. The Committee is of the opinion that DPE should have a mechanism in place to 
ensure that all their guidelines being issued from time to time are complied with by the 
CPSEs/Administrative Ministries/Departments.   The Committee notes that the 
Government has set a disinvestment target of Rs. 1.75 lakh crores and has decided to divest 
all PSEs which are not in the four strategic sectors identified by DIPAM, M/o Finance.  The 
Committee may be apprised of the revised mechanism for time bound closure o f loss 
making CPSEs and disposal of assets, once it is finalized.  The Committee also notes that in 
the coming years, more number of CPSEs in the non -strategic sectors and strategic sectors 
(except those in the four areas identified) will be divested/priva tized/merged/closed.  
Therefore, the number of employees likely to opt for VRS is also likely to increase.  
Therefore, Department should for esee this scenario and take appr opriate measures timely 
to impart their skill training under CRR Scheme to enable them to get re-deployment.

Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) 
 
95. As per Section 135 of the Com panies Act, 2013, all profit making corporates, including 
CPSEs exceeding threshold limits  prescribed in the Act having  net worth of Rs. 500 crore, or 
turnover of Rs. 1000 crore or net profit of Rs. 5 crore, are mandated to spend at least 2% of the 
average net profits (Profit Before Tax) of the company made during the three immediately 
preceding years to undertake CSR activities. Such companies have to constitute a CSR 
committee of the Board, comprising three or more Directors with at least one Independent 
Director. 
  
96. The Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014 notified by M/o Corporate Affairs and the 
Schedule VII of the Act lists the activities that can be undertaken under CSR. An advisory on 
observance of transparency and due diligence in selection and imp lementation of activities under 
CSR was issued by Department of Public Enterprises to the CPSEs in August, 2016. The 
Department has also issued guidelines on 10.12.2018  to all administrative Ministries & CPSEs 
for adopting a theme -based focused approach ev ery year on CSR expenditure by CPSEs. These 
guidelines inter alia provide that CSR expenditure for such thematic programmes should be 
around 60% of annual CSR expenditure of CPSEs. The aspirational districts identified by NITI 
Aayog may be given preference . The theme for 2019 -20 was School education, Healthcare and 
Nutrition and the theme identified for the FY 2020- 21 is „Health and Nutrition‟.

closure/disinvestment.   DPE should also maintain a data bank of skill trained VRS 
optees/dependents and explore the feasibility of displaying the information on their website 
so that interested CPSEs can approach them for redeployment, as the real success of the 
CRR Scheme can be gauged by the redeployment ratio.  
(Para 49) 
16. The Committee note s that DPE is consistently making efforts to increase 
redeployment rate under CRR scheme  and has been achieving the redeployment of about 
65% since last two years. The Committee recommend s that DPE in collaboration with   
NSDC, should hold frequent Job fairs in various states in respect of CRR beneficiaries to 
improve the redeployment percentage so that job opportunities are available for a larger 
number of beneficiaries and the objective of the scheme is fulfilled.  
(Para 50) 
17. The Committee is aware that every Ministry/Department has to earmark 10% of 
their total budget allocation of plan fund for North Eastern Region and Sikkim for the 
various developmental works/schemes for the benefit  of North Eastern Region and Sikkim. 
The Committee is further aware that the NER expenditure under Central Sector Schemes 
are being monitored every quarter jointly with M/o Development of NER to improve 
utilization of funds for NER under the Schemes. 
(Para 55) 
18. The Committee notes that for the Financial Year 2018 -19, both BE & RE allocation 
for RDC & CRR Schemes in the North -Eastern Region stood at Rs. 0.85 c rore.   Since AE 
was also Rs. 0.85 crore, DPE could utilize the entire amount during that year fo r RDC and 
CRR Schemes. 
(Para 56) 
19. However, during 2019 -20, AE was only Rs. 0.53 crore though both the BE & RE 
were Rs. 0.95 crore.  Therefore, DPE could spend only 56% of the allocated amount during 
the Financial Year 2019 -20.  During the Financial Year  2020-21, Rs. 1.05 crore was 
allocated as BE which was reduced to Rs. 0.56 crore at RE stage.  However, no expenditure 
was made under NER for both the Schemes during Financial Year 2020 -21, as no trainings 
could be conducted due to COVID -19 Pandemic.  For the Financial Year 2021 -22, Rs. 0.85 
crore has been allocated under NER for RDC & CRR Schemes.  Therefore, the Committee 
suggests that DPE should resume the trainings and conduct programmes in physical as well 
as virtual mode. The Committee is also of the view that under the CRR Scheme, all efforts 
should be made to identify more number of VRS optees/dependents in NER and  impart 
training to them to enhance their scope for redeployment.  Similarly, under the RDC 
Scheme also, more number of training programmes and workshops should be conducted to 

34 
 
enhance the optimum utilization of allocated budget even though the funds get transferred 
to non-lapsable pool, without getting lapsed. 
(Para 57) 
20. The Committee notes that CAPEX is an important component for moder nization 
expansion and diversification of CPSEs thereby improving the productivity of PSEs as well 
as economic growth of the country.  The Committee therefore suggests that DPE may 
continue to monitor the implementation of CAPEX activities of CPSEs regular ly.  DPE 
may also conduct more number of capacity building workshops on MoU System to sensitise 
CPSEs to leverage their net worth for CAPEX, as CAPEX is included as one of the 
parameters in the MoU evaluation system. 
(Para 62) 
21. The Committee further rec ommends that DPE should take appropriate steps to 
achieve the planned target of capital expenditure by CPSEs to revive the economy from the 
fallout of Covid-19 Pandemic.  
(Para 63) 
22. The purpose of MoU is to measure the performance of management of CPSEs  on 
key selected parameters against the targets agreed upon so as to improve the critical 
performance indicators of the organization.  It is an important tool being used by DPE for 
evaluating and monitoring the performance of CPSEs.  The Committee notes th at the 
number of MoUs signed during the Financial Year 2019 -20 and 2020 -21 was 144 and 124 
respectively. 
 
(Para 70) 
23. The Committee appreciates the new initiative taken by DPE to have a new 
framework for MoU System using a digital platform/dashboard for a self -driven MoU 
mechanism for the target setting and performance evaluation of CPSEs.  The Committee 
hopes that with the implementation of the New Framework and a digital dashboard with a 
centralized portal for entering, signing, monitoring and evaluatin g MoU agreements, the 
MoU System will be more simplified and transparent. 
(Para 71) 
24. The Committee hopes that the I nter Ministerial consultative process, together with 
DPE's role as a mentor and guide would facilitate the incipient sick and weak CPSEs i nto 
taking mid -term course , corrections so that they are saved from entering into the 'sick' 
bandwagon and likewise the 'weak' CPSEs would be able to nurse t hemselves back into 
good financial health.  
(Para 73) 

35 
 
 
 25. The Committee notes with concern that a  sizeable amount of land assets of CPSEs 
under closure are lying unsold/not transferred. The Committee recommends that DPE may 
use its good offices to impress upon the concerned administrative ministries to arrive at 
quick decisions so that these lands  could be utilized for useful purposes so as to become 
gainful and beneficial for the society at large, besides creating employment opportunities 
for the youth.  
(Para 79) 
26. The Committee is of the view that all efforts should be made to infuse the requisite  
capital into the CPSEs, so as to enable them to stand shoulder to shoulder with the private 
entities and offer stiff competition to them. The Committee feels that CPSEs had always 
played a vital role in unbundling privitisation sin ce a long time and thus deserve the much 
needed support. 
(Para 83) 
27. The Committee's view is that CPSEs are the backbone of the economy and there 
should be no stone left unturned to strengthen the CPSEs that are profit making and 
adding their contribution to the nation economic kitty.  The Committee also desires that it 
be apprised of the reasons as to why the reviving and restructuring mechanisms failed to 
have any positive effect on the loss making CPSEs.  
(Para 84) 
28. The Committee is of the opinion that DPE should have a me chanism in place to 
ensure that all their guidelines being issued from time to time are complied with by the 
CPSEs/Administrative Ministries/Departments.  The Committee notes that the 
Government has set a disinvestment target of Rs. 1.75 lakh crores and has decided to divest 
all PSEs which are not in the four strategic sectors identified by DIPAM, M/o Finance.  The 
Committee may be apprised of the revised mechanism for time bound closure of loss 
making CPSEs and disposal of assets, once it is finalized.  Th e Committee also notes that in 
the coming years, more number of CPSEs in the non -strategic sectors and strategic sectors 
(except those in the four areas identified) will be divested/privatized/merged/closed.  
Therefore, the number of employees likely to op t for VRS is also likely to increase.  
Therefore, Department should foresee this scenario and take appropriate measures timely 
to impart their skill training under CRR Scheme to enable them to get re-deployment. 
(Para 85) 
29. The Committee observes that  p rofessionalization of Boards of CPSEs plays a 
significant role in ensuring good corporate governance thereby promoting CPSEs to be 
more dynamic, competitive, performance oriented and viable in the market driven 
economy.  However, it is quite disheartening to note that around 480 positions of Non -
Official Directors (NOD) and 128  posts of senior officers including Functional  Directors 
are lying vacant on the Boards of various CPSEs as on date. The presence of NODs in the 

36 
 
Boards of CPSEs is essential to impro ve the functioning and effectiveness of the Board and 
to safeguard the interests of all stakeholders. 
(Para 91) 
30. The Committee strongly objects to the failure on the part of DPE to furnish the 
information regarding vacant posts of Directors to be filled  by PESB.  DPE brings out the 
Public Enterprises Survey every year & is also the nodal Department of all CPSEs.  Under 
such circumstances, DPE should have been prudent enough to make available  the 
information to the extent available, to the Committee for perusal. 
(Para 92) 
31. The Committee is dismayed by the increase in the number of vacant positions of 
Non-Official Directors of CPSEs from 313 in 2019 -20 to 480 in 2020 -21. Despite repeated 
recommendations made by the Committee in this regard, the Departmen t has not been 
proactive enough to get the huge number of vacant posts  filled up  which has a negative 
bearing on the effective functioning of the CPSEs.   The Committee feels disappointed by  
the inordinate delay in filling up such important positions, putti ng the effective functioning 
of CPSEs at stake.  The Committee therefore, recommends that DPE should play a more 
pro-active role and ensu re that vacancies of Directors o n the Boards of CPSEs do not 
remain vacant for more than six months  as any laid back ap proach in these matters would 
only jeopardize the growth of CPSEs as a whole.  The Department should desist in putting 
the complete onus on the Administrative Ministry/Department of the CPSEs or PESB.  The 
Committee further reiterates its earlier recommenda tion to include this as a parameter for 
MoU evaluation of CPSEs and impose penalty on such CPSEs wh ich do not fill up vacant 
posts of Directors in the Boards of CPSEs timely.  DPE should also chalk out a strategy to 
monitor the status of filling up of vaca ncies by the Search Committee/PESB/Management 
of CPSEs (in respect of below Board level posts). 
(Para 93) 
32. The Committee further recommends that a detailed exercise through a professional 
agency to assess the current status of implementation of various Human Resources (HR) 
development issues /activities in CPSEs should be conducted and best practices be 
identified  and replicated in CPSEs, as had been done by the Department earlier. 
(Para 94) 
33. The Committee is aware that under the Section 135 of the Co mpanies Act, 2013, 
CSR (Corporate Social Responsibility) activities have been made mandatory for all profit 
making CPSEs to allocate 2% of their average net profits (NBT) of the three preceding 
years. Further as per the latest guidelines issued by the DPE vide their OM dated 10 th 
December, 2018, the CPSEs are to utilise the CSR Fund in a focussed manner towards 
national priorities by adopting a theme based approach each year. The Committee  
understands that most of the contributions to the PM CARES Fund by t he CPSEs have 
been made from their CSR Funds diverting a large share that would have otherwise been 
utilised towards theme based CSR activities in the local areas.   The Committee therefore, 

37 
 
desires that the CSR Fund should be utilised to meet the targets s et for the theme based 
activities in the respective area and aspirational districts as spelt out in the guidelines. 
(Para 100) 
34. The Committee notes that CSR expen diture during the year 2019 -20 wa s much 
higher i.e. Rs. 5066.93 crore than the previous Fin ancial Year 2018 -19.  The Committee 
suggests that the CPSEs should utilize the CSR fund mainly for undertaking activities 
related to „Health & Nutrition‟, the theme identified during Financial Year 2020 -21, for 
focused intervention by CPSEs under CSR.  The Committee further recommends that DPE 
should also maintain information regarding the activities undertaken by CPSEs under 
CSR fund as it is a parameter for MoU evaluation & DPE is the nodal Department for all 
CPSEs.  Further, M/o Corporate Affairs may be impressed upon to involve local 
representatives in the project selection.  The Committee further is of the view that a set of 
statutory rules/guidelines may be framed or incorporated in the current rules ibid wherein 
it becomes mandatory to seek the opinion  of the local area representative before 
finalizing/implementing a scheme under CSR. The Committee is also of the view that more 
number of training programmes on CSR should be included in the RDC Scheme to enable 
CPSEs to undertake the right kind of activities under CSR.  
(Para 101) 
35. The Committee further recommends that CPSEs should fulfill the social objective of 
removing regional disparities in the count ry and should, therefore, also focus  their CSR 
expenditure in geographically remote and backward areas of the country, in addition to the 
Aspirational Districts. The Committee further desires that CPSEs should use their 
innovative ideas and management skills for environmental protection.  
(Para 102) 
36. The Committee observes that the Department has tak en initiatives to conduct 
studies in diverse areas. However, the Committee is surprised to note that no study has 
been conducted to assess the impact of Covid -19 on CPSEs, despite the fact that DPE is the 
nodal Department of all the CPSEs.  The Committee, therefore, is of the considered opinion 
that a detailed study needs to be conducted to comprehend at micro-level, the actual impact 
of COVID -19 pandemic and subsequent lockdowns on the performance of the CPSEs so 
that necessary in tervention by the Governme nt could  be made to mitigate the economic 
fallout.  
 (Para 104)
