iii. Further, the Central Government has been empowered to exclusively auction 
mining lease and composite licence for 24 critical minerals listed in the new Part-D 
of the First Schedule to the said Act which includes the mineral Lithium. 
iv. The objective of the said amendment is to increase exploration and mining of 
critical minerals including Lithium and ensure self -sufficiency in supply of critical 
minerals which are essential for the advancement of many sectors, including high - 
tech electronics, telecommunications, transport and defence. They are also vital to 
power the transition to a low -emission economy, and the renewable technologie s 
that will be required to meet the „Net Zero‟ commitment of India by 2070. 
v. The auction of critical and strategic minerals brings several key benefits, 
including bolstering domestic production, reducing import dependency, promoting 
sustainable resource man agement, attracting investments in the mining sector and 
the development of key industries crucial for India's industrial and technological 
advancement. This is a step towards creating a reliable supply chain of these 
mineral and making an „Atma  Nirbhar Bharat‟ and contribute towards increased 
economic growth. 
vi. The Central Government has launched the first tranche of e -auction of 20 
mineral blocks of critical and strategic minerals on 29.11.2023 which includes two 
blocks of Lithium and associated minerals for grant of composite licence which on 
completion of G2 level of exploration followed by production aims to ensure 
steady supply of these minerals, thus reducing our reliance on imports and ensuring 
a more secure and resilient supply chain. 

20 
 
vii. Besides auction of critical minerals by the Central Government, in order to 
further boost exploration of critical and deep -seated minerals, a new mineral 
concession namely, exploration licence has been introduced for 29 critical and 
deep-seated minerals. Critical and d eep-seated minerals such as Cobalt, Lithium, 
Nickel, Gold, Silver, and Copper are difficult to explore and mine as compared to 
surfacial or bulk minerals. The country is mostly dependent on imports of these 
minerals. The exploration licence granted through auction shall permit the licencee 
to undertake reconnaissance and prospecting operations for critical and deep-seated 
minerals mentioned in the newly inserted Seventh Schedule to the MMDR Act. 
viii. Exploration license aims to create an enabling mechanism where in the Junior 
Mining Companies will bring in expertise from across the world in acquisition, 
processing and interpretation of exploration data and leverage the risk -taking 
ability in discovery of deep -seated mineral deposits through adoption of expertise 
and latest technologies. 
ix. KABIL, a Joint venture between 3 central PSE of Ministry of Mines has 
signed a Moll with CAMYEN, Govt. Company in Catamarca province of 
Argentina on 29.12.2020 to explore sourcing of lithium and other mineral assets in 
Argentina. Subsequently, KABIL has entered into an agreement with CAMYEN 
on 15.01.2024 to start its first ever Exploration and Development project for 
Lithium exploration followed by exploitation of 5 lithium blocks covering an area 
of 15000 ha in Catamarca province of  Argentina. All the above measures are 
aimed to ensure that India will become Atma  Nirbhar in the field of Lithium -ion 
battery manufacturing to facilitate transition to Electric mobility. 
 
PUBLIC AWARENESS & PROMOTION OF EV 
Recommendation/Observation 
20. For the promotion and penetration of Electric Vehicles, creating awareness 
regarding the environmental and economic benefits of adoption/migration to 
Electric Vehicles among the people is necessary. It's equally important to convey 
the initiatives taken by  the Central & State governments to promote e -mobility in 
the country. The Committee recommends that awareness campaigns, events, etc. at 
the local level in coordination with urban local bodies/municipalities, etc. should 
be organised in the regional langu ages in the States to promote Electric Vehicles 
and their wide acceptance by general public. Print, Audio Video, Radio, and 
Social Media modes should also be utilized to enhance the outreach.                                     
 (Para 117) 

21 
 
 
 
Action Taken Replies 
NITI Aayog's  Shoonya campaign is already a successful template for outreach 
enhancement aimed at swift EV adoption by multiple stakeholders. 
 
EV PENETRATION & GIG ECONOMY 
Recommendation/Observation 
21. According to a report of NITI Aayog, Indian Gig force is expected to rise to 
23.5 million by 2029 -30, from the current workforce of 7.7 million. Most of the 
delivery start -ups especially in food & grocery delivery employ gig force on a 
large scale, which c ould be a potential driving agent for increasing the Electric 
Vehicles penetration in the country, particularly in 2 -Wheeler segment. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should take steps in coordination with 
the stakeholders to make the vehicle fle et of 2 -Wheelers in these start -
ups/companies mandatorily to be Electric Vehicles in order to achieve the 30 per 
cent target of EV penetration by the year 2030.  
(Para 118) 
Action Taken Replies 
Noted. NITI Aayog's Shoonya campaign also focuses on Gig Industry and delivery 
ecosystem. 
 
ELECTRIC VEHICLE (EV) SUBSIDIES & FAME-II SCHEME 
Recommendation/Observation 
21. The Committee observes that in phase -2 of FAME Scheme, only 9 major 
cities having population of over 4 million were targeted in aggregation model for 
e-buses and very few States have earlier participated in operational cost model. 
With the announcement of PM e -Bus Sewa, the Committee is hopeful that the 
Scheme will help transform urban mobility landscape in smaller cities also. The 
Committee recommends that the concerned Ministry  (ies) should strive for the 
early implementation of the scheme so that the ben efits of the scheme will 
proliferate in an efficient manner and timely.         
  (Para 121) 

22 
 
Action Taken Replies 
NITI Aayog has noted.  PM e-Bus Sewa Scheme covers deployment of 10,000 e -
buses in 169 Indian cities. CESL is aggregating the demand for this scheme and 
consent on Payment Security Mechanism (PSM) is mandatory for states to avail 
benefits of this scheme. In line with this, MHI is working on Payment Security 
Mechanism (PSM) scheme to address monthly payment defaults by Public 
Transport Authorities (PTAs) to Original Equipment Manufacturers 
(OEMs)/operators. For this purpose, MHI has carried out multiple stakeholder 
consultations involving concerned ministries/departments, PTAs, private operators, 
financing institution, fund donors etc. Based on this, the proposal was prepared. 
The proposal for seeking approval as per rules is under process. 
 

23 
 
CHAPTER–III 
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH 
THE COMMITTEE HAS NOT ACCEPTED THE REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY 
ELECTRIC VEHICLE SUBSIDY & FAME SCHEME 
Recommendation/Observation 
22. The Committee notes that initially the Government had the target of 
supporting 55,000 e -4 Wheelers under the FAME II Scheme, but the revised 
targets have reduced the number of vehicles to the committed funds only i.e. for 
11,000 e -4 Wheelers. Though 2 Whee lers is a dominant category, share of 4 
Wheelers is also significant in the automotive sector of the country. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should increase the number of electric vehicles to be 
supported in the 4 Wheelers category and also inc lude private e-4 Wheelers in the 
domain of FAME II Scheme with a cap based on the cost and battery capacity of 
the vehicle.  
(Para 26) 
Action Taken Replies 
With greater emphasis on providing affordable and environmentally friendly public 
transportation options for the masses, the scheme is applicable mainly to vehicles 
used for public transport or those registered for commercial purposes in 3W, 4W 
and Bus segm ents. However, privately owned registered 2Ws are covered under 
the scheme as a mass segment.  
Therefore, the number of supported EVs under the e -4W segment remained lower. 
The details of supported EVs under FAME India Scheme Phase -II as on 
15.03.2024 are as under: 
Vehicle type Total No. of Vehicles supported under FAME-II 
2-wheeler 13,07,047 
3-wheeler 1,50,934 
4-wheeler 19,028 
Total 14,77,009 
                Source: https://fame2.heavyindustries.gov.in/dashboard.aspx 
 

24 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the Ministry should 
increase the number of electric vehicles to be supported in the 4 Wheelers and 
also include private e-4 wheelers in FAME-II or yet to be approved FAME III 
Scheme. Further, the Committee feels that emphasis should be given to  
publicity of the long -term benefits of e -vehicles to impact a wide outreach 
while popularizing the schemes of the Government to pr omote transition to 
electric mobility in the country. 
 
PUBLIC TRANSPORT & CHARGING INFRASTRUCTURE 
Recommendation/Observation 
23. Electric Vehicles have range constraints as its range depends on battery 
capacity and therefore, the vehicles need charging at frequent intervals, whereas 
ICE Vehicles have a fuel tank which gives them range advantage vis -a-vis electric 
vehicles. The Commi ttee recommends that Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas 
should also consider including the sub -urban and rural areas under the target 
areas for establishing Charging Stations, as installations of charging stations only 
at retail outlets of Oil Marketing C ompanies would not be adequate due to range 
anxiety in case of electric vehicles. Further, in view of the targeted Electric 
Charging Stations of 22,000, the sanctioned Charging Stations of 7,432 for 
installation under FAME -II is way below the target and, t herefore the Committee 
recommends that sincere efforts should be made for setting up of more Charging 
Stations to address the issue of range anxiety and boost the EV penetration in the 
automotive sector in the country. 
 (Para 73) 
Action Taken Replies 
As pe r the information received from Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas 
(MoPNG), Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) have targeted to set up 22,000 
Charging stations by December, 2024.  Ministry of Heavy Industries under FAME-
II Subsidy scheme have also granted a subsidy of Rs.800 crore to OMCs for setting 
up 7432 fast EV chargers which is a part of overall target of setting up 22000 EV 
chargers.  Rest of the charging stations i.e. 14,568 will be set up by OMCs with 
their own capex without any subsidy.  As on 01.01. 2024, OMCs have provided 
10,771 EV charging Stations (IOCL – 7394, BPCL-975 and HPCL-2402).  Further, 
as per advice from the committee, OMCs will also set up charging stations in sub -
urban and rural areas within overall target of 22,000 charging stations. 

25 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Heavy Industries should 
explore the possibility of setting up more charging stat ions in suburban and 
rural areas beyond the overall target of 22000 charging station to address the 
issue of Range Anxiety of EV's in the country  for which, a relook in the 
budgetary projection may be made in a holistic manner. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
24. The Committee was informed by the Ministry of Heavy Industries that 520 
Charging Stations had been sanctioned under the Phase -I of FAME India Scheme. 
Further, 2,877 charging stations in 68 cities across 25 States/UTs and 1576 
charging stations across 9 Expressways and 16 Highways have been sanctioned 
under FAME-II India Scheme. The Committee recommends that other Ministries 
should be roped in along with charging infrastructure operators to put in place a 
comprehensive plan for establishment of a Charging Network in the country to 
address the issue of road anxiety of electric vehicle owners.       
  (Para 74) 
Action Taken Replies 
Heavy Industries has consulted and roped in the Ministry of Power (MoP), 
Ministry of Road Transport & Highways (MoRTH) and Ministry of Petroleum & 
Natural Gas (MoPNG) for comprehensive plan for establishment of a Chargi ng 
Network in the country. 
Ministry of Heavy Industries has sanctioned Rs.800 crore  as capital subsidy to the 
three Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) namely Indian Oil Corporation Limited 
(IOCL), Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL) and Bharat Petroleum 
Corporation Limited (BPCL) of the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas 
(MoPNG) for establishment of 7,432 electric vehicle public charging stations. 
These OMCs will setup the charging stations at their retail outlets spread across the 
length and breadth of the country. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
The Committee while apprecia ting the role of the Ministry of Heavy 
Industries, feel that there is a  pressing need to put in place a comprehensive 
plan for establishment of charging network in the country and reiterates it 
recommendation for putting in place such a comprehensive plan to address 
the issue of road anxiety of electric vehicle owners. 

26 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
25. The Committee is of the view that one of the biggest barriers to the 
widespread adoption of Electric Vehicles remains the lack of charging 
infrastructure and the overall time required to charge such batteries. With a 
Battery Swapping System, EV owners will save on the high cost of buying a new set 
of battery at periodic intervals as they can simply replace the exhausted batteries 
for fully charged ones at Battery Swapping Stations. The Committee recommends 
that the Ministry of Heavy Industries should conduc t a study regarding the 
feasibility of battery standardisation and formulate a stable Battery Swapping 
Policy with the highest levels of safety standards that can infuse confidence in 
consumer’s decision making thereby boosting demand whilst inducing 
infrastructure build -out by swapping operators, which has a huge potential to 
invite FDI into the battery swapping network creation in the country.  
(Para 77) 
Action Taken Replies 
As per the information received from NITI Aayog, it is informed that Battery 
swapping is an alternative to charging the Electric Vehicle which involves 
exchanging discharged batteries for charged ones. Battery swapping is popularly 
used for smaller vehicles such as 2 and 3 wheelers which have smaller batteries. 
Battery Swapping is already operational in India and more new swapping stations 
are coming up every year in the country. While stakeholder discussions with a 
wide spectrum of stakeholders representing Battery Swapping Operators, Battery 
Manufacturers, Vehicle OEMs, Financial Institutions, CSOs, Think Tanks and 
other experts have been held, it may be noted that Electric Vehicles' battery 
ecosystem is a complex domain involving variety of technologies which are still 
evolving.  It must also be noted that India's present Battery Swapping practice is as 
per global best practices. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
The Committee while appreciating that the present Battery Swapping practice 
in India is as per global best practices, reiterates it s recommendation that in 
near future Ba ttery swapping P olicy s hould be conceptualized and 
implemented to ensure consumer confidence in Electric Vehicles. 
 
 

27 
 
MANUFACTURING AND INDUSTRY DEVELOPMENT: LI- BATTERIES 
Recommendation/Observation 
26. The Committee is of the view that one of the major challenges to make 
electric vehicles more affordable and economical to operate is their high 
ownership cost vis -a-vis ICE vehicles, as  the electric vehicles include a battery 
pack that forms about 40 -45 per cent of their ownership cost. Since the Lithium -
ions Batteries (LIBs) for electric vehicles has a greater durability with relatively 
high energy and power density, the Committee recommends that Government 
should explore the possibility of shrinking further the GST on Lithium-ion batteries 
to bring down the ownership cost of electric vehicles. Further, there is a need to 
address the issue of GST for manufacturers as well in order to reduce the high cost 
of electric vehicles and consequently its affordabili ty for the potential buyers to 
promote faster adoption of electric vehicles.  
(Para 83) 
Action Taken Replies 
As per the information received from the Department of Revenue, Ministry of 
Finance, the GST rates and exemptions are based on the recommendation of the 
GST Council, accordingly, the issues of GST rate reduction on batteries for electric 
vehicles (EV) and parts of EVs was placed before the Council in its 52nd and 47th 
Meeting respectively, however no changes have been recommended by the Council 
in this regard. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Heavy Industries should 
relentlessly pursue  the issue of GST rate reduction with the D/o Revenue, 
keeping in  view the greater good which would result in reduction in cost of 
electric vehicles and also help Government meeting its zero emission targets 
within the time frame set for the same. 
 
ELECTRIC VEHICLE (EV) SUBSIDIES AND INCENTIVES 
Recommendation/Observation 
27. The Committee notes the challenges associated with financing the Electric 
Vehicles and is hopeful that the efforts of NITI Aayog, World Bank and SIDBI will 
be helpful in addressing the issue of finance availability for the potential EV 
buyers. Taking into consideration the efforts of the Government for promoting 
Electric Vehicles and green asset creation, the Committee recommends that 

28 
 
Electric Vehicles should be brought under the Priority Sector Lending (PSL) 
category until the 30 per cent penetration targe t fixed for 2030 is achieved, for 
accelerating India’s commitment towards net-zero emissions. Further, cooperation 
between EV Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) and lenders may be 
encouraged to improve EV buyers accessibility to finance. Ministry of H eavy 
Industries may also consider including private EV Four Wheelers in FAME -II so 
as to improve their share in the Electric Mobility Mission.                           
(Para 108) 
Action Taken Replies 
NITI Aayog will engage with RBI and Ministry of Finance  on this 
recommendation of DRPSC for treating EVs as Priority Sector Landing (PSL) 
Category. 
Further, the FAME-II scheme is ending on 31.03.2024 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
The Ministry , in  early part of this report had replied Electric mobility 
promotion scheme 2024 has been notified for a period of 4 months, w.e.f 
01.04.2024 to 31.07.2024  and FAME III has been formulated for approval. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may consider 
including Four Wheelers in the FAME III so as to improve their share in 
Electric Mobility Mission. 
 
MANUFACTURING & INDUSTRY DEVELOPMENT : INTERNATIONAL 
COOPERATION 
Recommendation/Observation 
28. The Committee notes the achievements of Schemes such as PLI -Auto and 
National Programme on ACC, but until the benefits of these schemes spread across 
the country and self-sufficiency in manufacturing of batteries and auto components 
is achieved, the Govern ment should ensure adequate supply of components, cells 
and batteries for growth of Electric Vehicles vis -à-vis ICE Vehicles. The 
Committee recommends the Ministry to foster international 
cooperation/partnership with global suppliers/countries to ensure an d maintain 
the supply chain requirements of the domestic Electric Vehicle industry. Ministry 
of Heavy Industries should also work in coordination with the Ministry of Micro, 
Small and Medium Enterprises to help develop a Manufacturing Network for 

29 
 
manufacture of Battery and EV components and progress in this regard may be 
shared with the Committee.                  
 (Para 114) 
Action Taken Replies 
NITI Aayog has noted.  
As per the extent policy and guidelines of Government of India there is no 
restriction on import of raw materials, components, child parts of conventional led 
acid cells and Advance Chemistry Cell (ACC). As regards, maintaining the supply 
chains requirements of the domestic Electric Vehicle Industry, the Indian cell and 
Battery Manufacturers are individually entering into supply, technology transfer 
etc. agreement with foreign counter parts. Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) has 
been assisting the Indian companies in getting VISA for their foreign employees 
for their visit to India to install, commission etc. machinery equipments supplied 
by overseas partners. The Ministry of Heavy Industries makes efforts to foster 
global partnership with suppliers/ countries to enable cooperation in the auto sector 
including supply chain of EVs and cells. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
The Committee while appreciating the steps taken towards maintaining the 
supply chain requirements of the domestic Electric Vehicle Industry, 
reiterates its recommendation that Ministry of Heavy Industries should work 
in coor dination with  medium Enterprises to help develop a Manufacturing 
Network for manufacture of Battery and EV components. 
  

30 
 
CHAPTER–IV 
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH 
THE FINAL REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY ARE STILL AWAITED 
 
ELECTRIC VEHICLE SUBSIDY & FAME SCHEME 
Recommendation/Observation 
29. The Committee notes that the initial targets were revised by bringing down 
the number of vehicles to be supported under the FAME-II Scheme. The Committee 
is of the opinion that in order to facilitate the transition momentum to Electric 
Mobility, more numbe r of electric vehicles need to be supported and, therefore 
recommends that the Ministry should broaden the scope and extend the FAME -II 
Scheme for at least 3 more years in consultation with the Industry stakeholders to 
make the Scheme more inclusive.  
(Para 25) 
Action Taken Replies 
Initially, FAME India Scheme Phase-II was launched by Government of India for a 
period of three (3) years commencing from 01.04.2019, with an outlay of 
Rs.10,000 crore. After various stakeholders  consultations including with the auto 
industry, FAME India Phase II scheme has been extended for a period of two (2) 
years i.e. up to 31.03.2024. 
Further, to make the scheme more inclusive, the outlay of the scheme has been 
enhanced from Rs.10,000 crore to Rs.11,500 crore. 
The Scheme for Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Electric Vehicles in India 
Phase III (FAME -III) for promotion of Electric Mobility in the country with an 
outlay of Rs.10,000 crore over the period of two years has been formulated by t his 
Ministry. The proposal for seeking approval as per rules is under process. 
 
Electric Mobility Promotion Scheme -2024 (EMPS) – After review of the FAME -
II, Electric Mobility Promotion Scheme -2024 has been notified vide S.O. 1334(E) 
dated 13.03.2024 with an outlay of Rs.500 crore to be implemented over a period 
of 4 months, w.e.f. 01.04.2024 to 31.07.2024, for faster adoption of electric two 
wheeler (e -2W) and three wheeler (e -3W) to provide further impetus to the 
mobility and development of electric vehic le (EV) manufacturing eco -system in 
the country.           
 

31 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
The Committee has been informed during its meeting with the Ministry on 
07.10.2024 that the PM-E Drive Scheme, implemented from 01.10.2024 by the 
Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI), has replaced FAME -III and is expected 
to provide enhanced support for the adoption of electric vehicles and the 
development of necessary charging infrastructure. However, the Committee 
expresses its co ncerns regarding the rationale behind launching the PM -E 
Drive Scheme. Despite the successful implementation of FAME -I and FAME-
II, which have garnered significant popularity and familiarity among the 
target beneficiaries, the Government have launched PM-E Drive with similar 
objectives, a budget outlay of ₹10,900 crore (comparable to the proposed 
₹10,000 crore for FAME -III), and largely similar components. The 
Committee is concerned that this may create confusion among the 
beneficiaries, as the new scheme more or less mirrors the objectives of FAME-
III except minor new features like Face- Recognition and E- Vouchers.  
Moreover, FAME-III was scheduled to be rolled out in August 2024  and the 
launch of the PM-E Drive Scheme has resulted in an unnecessary delay of two 
months. In the light of this, the Committee calls for a comprehensive 
explanation regarding the need to introduce the PM -E Drive Scheme, 
especially considering the existing popularity and famili arity of the FAME 
Schemes, which has a very similar sco pe and components, albeit under a 
different name. The Committee seeks clarification on the reasons for this shift 
and the potential implications for the beneficiaries.

CHAPTER 1 
INTRODUCTION 
 
The Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI)  is crucial in driving industrial growth, fostering 
technological advancements, and promoting self -reliance in the manufacturing sector. It 
formulates policies and implements schemes to strengthen key industries such as the automotive, 
heavy engineering equipment and machine tools, and heavy electrical industries.  
The automotive sector, a key pillar of the economy, contributes 6.8% to India’s GDP and 
accounts for 40% of the manufacturing GDP. The capital goods sector, comprising heavy 
engineering equipment and machine  tools, constitutes 12% of the total manufacturing output, 
translating to 1.8% of GDP. The heavy electrical industry further adds a 1% share to the GDP. 
Given their substantial contributions, these sectors play a vital role in India's economic growth 
and industrial development. 
 
Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) 
 
2. The Ministry administers three key industry sectors: the Automotive Industry, including 
Tractor and earth -moving equipment; the Heavy Engineering Equipment and Machine Tools 
Industry (HE&MT); a nd the Heavy Electrical Industry (HEI). It also administers 21 central 
public sector enterprises (CPSEs) and four autonomous bodies. Out of the 21 CPSEs, 16 are 
operational. The remaining 4 CPSEs are under closure, and one is non-operational.

22. The MHI informed that the Government launched a new scheme titled "PM Electric 
Drive Revolution in Innovative Vehicle Enhancement (PM E-DRIVE)" from 1st October 2024 for 
two years. The earlier Electric Mobility Promotion Scheme (EMPS -2024), which was 
implemented from 1st April 2024 to 30 th September 2024, has been subsumed under the PM E -
DRIVE scheme. Consequently, the PM E-DRIVE scheme is effective from 1 st April 2024 to 31st 
March 2026 with a total outlay of  Rs. 10,900 crore. For the financial year  2025-26, a budgetary 
allocation of Rs. 4000 crore has been made for this scheme. 
23. The primary objective of the PM E-DRIVE scheme is to expedite the adoption of EVs by 
providing upfront incentives for their purchase  and by facilitating the establishment of essential 
charging infrastructure for EVs. The scheme also promotes mass mobility by supporting mean s 
of public transportation. The scheme aims to promote EVs to reduce the environmental impact of 
transportation, fuel security and improve air quality.

Status of e-Buses under PM E-DRIVE 
34. The Ministry informed the Committee that initially the scheme will cover 9 major cities 
(Mumbai, Delhi, Bangalore, Hyderabad, Ahmedabad, Chennai, Kolkata, Surat and Pune) having  
the population more than 40 lakh. CESL is the implementing agency and issued an Expression of 
Interest (EOI) on 13 th November 2024, with the submission deadline set for 20th February 2025. 
To secure funds, States must register a Direct Debit Mandate (DDM) with the RBI . So far, 
Karnataka and Telangana have submitted their DDMs. 

12 
 
35. The Committee observes that, at the initial stage, the Scheme covers only major 
cities with populations exceeding 40 lakh. Given India’s vast geography and the pressing 
need to reduce fossil fuel imports and vehicular air pollution, limiting e -bus deployment to 
a few large cities will not be sufficient to address these challenges comprehensively. 
Therefore, it recommends that the Ministry expand the scope of the Scheme to include 
smaller cities. If necessary, the Ministry should seek additional budgetary alloc ations at the 
Revised Estimates (RE) stage from the Ministry of Finance to maximize the Scheme’s 
potential in promoting electric bus adoption and green energy transition.

48. Electric vehicles run on batteries; currently, most of the batteries and associated raw 
materials are imported from China. As announced in the Union Budget 2025 -26, the 
Government's recent exemption of customs duties on 35 additional capital goods essential for 
lithium-ion battery manufacturing is poised to significantly impact the automotive industry 
regarding the use of indigenous advan ced chemistry cells.  As Lithium -Ion Cell manufacturing 
technology is a niche technology, currently not fully developed in India, the Cell manufacturers 
are required to invest heavily , including on import of the latest Capital Goods required for 
manufacturing of ACCs. Due to lack of indigenous sourcing of capital goods, only way to get a 
competitive edge is by exempting customs duties on such critical  Capital Goods. The duty 
exemptions complement the PLI ACC scheme by incentivising domestic manufacturing of ACC 
technologies. This synergy is anticipated to strengthen India's position in the global EV market, 
making the country's automotive sector more competitive internationally.  
 
49. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Heavy Industries implement the 
recent customs duty exemptions on 35 additional capital goods essential for lithium -ion 
battery manufacturing. Given India's reliance on battery imports, particularly from China, 
and the high investment required for ACC production, these exemptions wi ll provide a 
competitive edge to domestic manufacturers. Additionally, their alignment with the PLI 
ACC scheme is expected to boost indigenous manufacturing, reduce import dependence, 
and enhance India’s position in the global EV market.  
 
50. The Committee notes the significant changes in the Mines and Minerals (Regulation 
and Development) [MMRD] Amendment Act, 2023 *. The amendments to the Act enables 
participation of private companies in mining exploration by providing them with 
exploration license for reconnaissance and prospecting of critical minerals. The Committee 
is hopeful that the participation of private players will expedite the exploration and mining 
of critical minerals like lithium without technological constraints. This is expected to 
strengthen indigenous manufacturing of lithium -ion batteries for electric vehicles and 
reduce dependence on imports of critical minerals.

1. The Committee observes with dismay  that the Ministry could not fully utilise its 
allocated budget for the previous two financial years i.e. 2022 -23 and 2023 -24. In 2022-23,

adheres to the Monthly Expenditure Plan (MEP)  and Quarterly Expenditure Plan (QEP) 
to ensure proper and timely utilisation.

the adoption of electric buses and electric trucks continues to be limited. To accelerate this 
transition and work towards the country’s ambitious goal of 35% of total vehicle sales  
being electric by 2030, it recommends that the Ministry enhance policy support through 
targeted financial incentives, expansion of charging infrastructure particularly for e -2Ws 
and e-4Ws and promotion of localized manufacturing of key EV components. Addi tionally, 
a strategic focus on high -utilization segments like e -buses and e -trucks is crucial to 
decarbonizing commercial transport. 
(Para 33) 
 
13. The Committee observes that, at the initial stage, the Scheme covers only major 
cities with populations exce eding 40 lakh. Given India’s vast geography and the pressing 
need to reduce fossil fuel imports and vehicular air pollution, limiting e -bus deployment to 
a few large cities will not be sufficient to address these challenges comprehensively. 
Therefore, it recommends that the Ministry expand the scope of the Scheme to include 
smaller cities. If necessary, the Ministry should seek additional budgetary allocations at the 
Revised Estimates (RE) stage from the Ministry of Finance to maximize the Scheme’s 
potential in promoting electric bus adoption and green energy transition.  
(Para 35) 
14.   The Committee emphasises that charging infrastructure is crucial for successfully 
transitioning to electric mobility. A meagre Rs. 180.00 crore was allocated  at the RE stage 
for 2024 -25 for installing EV public charging stations across the country, and the entire 
amount remains unutilised. It recommends that the Ministry proactively seek enhanced 
funding from the Ministry of Finance at the RE stage (2025 -26) to expedite the installation 
of charging infrastructure under the PM E -DRIVE, thereby providing a much -needed 
boost to electric mobility. 
(Para 38) 
15. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Heavy Industries finalize 
guidelines and SOPs to ensure the swift and effective implementation of the PM e-Bus Sewa 
Payment Security Mechanism (PSM) Scheme. It is crucial to expedite coordination with 
States to  facilitate the registration of Direct Debit Mandates (DDMs) with the RBI, 
ensuring wider participation beyond Karnataka and Telangana. Additionally, the Ministry 

28 
 
should establish a robust monitoring mechanism to track implementation progress and 
address any challenges stakeholders face to enhance the scheme’s effectiveness. 
(Para 40) 
 
16.  The Committee was informed that the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme 
for Automobile and Auto Components is expected to attract an  investment of 
approximately Rs. 42,500 crore and generate around 1.48 lakh direct employment 
opportunities over five years. As on 19.02.2025, total 77 variants of Champion Original 
Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) and 39 variant of Component Champion OEMs, both 
overseas and Indian, have been approved under the components of this scheme.  As per 
data provided by the Ministry of Heavy Industries, the actual expenditure under the 
scheme for financial year 2024 -25 up to 31 st January 2025 stands at Rs. 246.21 cror e, 
representing approximately 70.98% of the allocated funds. Given the critical role of this 
scheme in strengthening domestic manufacturing under the Make in India  and 
Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiatives, the Committee recommends that the funds allocated at the 
Revised Estimate (RE) stage be fully utilized by the end of the current financial year.  
(Para 43) 
 
17.  The scheme's budget rose sharply in 2024 -25, but actual expenditure remains below 
RE, highlighting utilisation challenges. For 2025-26, a budget allo cation of ₹155.76 crore 
has been proposed.  The Committee believes this scheme facilitates realising  the goal of 
Make in India and Atmnirbhar Bharat by promoting newer and niche technologies . It needs 
to be implemented promptly and effectively with robust zeal. Therefore, it is recommended 
that the scheme's implementation be streamlined to ensure efficient fund utilisation, timely 
disbursement, and alignment with industry demand to maximize its impact on domestic 
battery manufacturing.  
(Para 47) 
18. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Heavy Industries implement the 
recent customs duty exemptions on 35 additional capital goods essential for lithium -ion 
battery manufacturing. Given India's reliance on battery imports, particularly from China, 
and th e high investment required for ACC production, these exemptions will provide a 
competitive edge to domestic manufacturers. Additionally, their alignment with the PLI 
ACC scheme is expected to boost indigenous manufacturing, reduce import dependence, 
and enhance India’s position in the global EV market.  
(Para 49) 
 
 

29 
 
19. The Committee notes the significant changes in the Mines and Minerals (Regulation 
and Development) [MMRD] Amendment Act, 2023 *. The amendments to the Act enables 
participation of private companies in mining exploration by providing them with 
exploration license for reconnaissance and p rospecting of critical minerals. The Committee 
is hopeful that the participation of private players will expedite the exploration and mining 
of critical mine rals like lithium without technological constraints. This is expected to 
strengthen indigenous manufacturing of lithium -ion batteries for electric vehicles and 
reduce dependence on imports of critical minerals. 
(Para 50) 
 
20. The Committee recommends regular assessment and monitoring of Phase II of the 
Scheme for Enhancement of Competitiveness in the Indian Capital Goods Sector  to ensure 
its effective implementation, with a focus on strengthening domestic manufacturing 
capabilities and reducing reliance on imported high -end machines. This will help foster a 
globally competitive and self-reliant capital goods industry.  
(Para 57) 
 
21. The Committee notes with concern the drastic reduction in Budget Estimates (BE) 
for 2025 -26 to Rs. 120.00 crore from Rs. 250.00 crore in previous two financial years, 
raising questions about the Ministry’s ability to implement key initiatives effectively. The 
shortage of funds poses a significant challenge to the execution of schemes. It recommends 
that the Ministry address funding shortfalls at the Revised Estimates (RE) stage to prevent 
underutilisation. Furthermore, the Committee observes that no allocations have been made 
for industry associations and public sector undertakings (PSUs) to support the capital 
goods sector. Given the crucial role of these entities in promoting Government schemes and 
raising stakeholder awareness, the Committee urges the Min istry to engage with the 
Ministry of Finance to reassess and enhance budgetary provisions for these essential 
activities. 
(Para 59) 
 
22. The Committee notes that among the 04 autonomous bodies under the Ministry, only 
the Central Manufacturing Technology I nstitute (CMTI) has been allocated funds in the BE 
for FY 2025 -26, while no provision has been made for the other 03 autonomous bodies. Given 
the critical importance of R&D and technological upgradation in maintaining global 
competitiveness, it recommends that the Ministry extend its focus to other R&D institutions 
and ensure they receive adequate budgetary support for technological advancement. 
Furthermore, the budget allocated to CMTI, Bengaluru, should be utilised efficiently to achieve 
the intended outcomes. The Ministry may consider seeking an enhancement at the RE stage if 
additional funds are required. 
(Para 61) 

30 
 
23. The Committee observed that out of the 16 Operational CPSEs under the 
administrative control of the Ministry of Heavy Industries, 6 2 CPSEs are loss making 
CPSEs. It has also been observed that HEC is a loss-making enterprise continuously for the 
past several years. However, considering the recent performance of HEC, there seems to be 
potential for its revival if immediate measures are taken. It recommends that the Ministry 
should make concerted efforts to improve the situation of HEC and assess the reasons as to 
why the loss making CPSEs have increased from 5 to 6. The Ministry may develop strategic 
steps to revive the CPSEs and accordingly consider allocating funds at RE stage.  
(Para 64) 
 
24. The Committee notes that the number of Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) 
under the control of the Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) is decreasing year after year. 
The Committee recommends  that the Ministry work towards enhancing the performance 
of CPSEs under its control and adopt restructuring measures to revive the loss -making 
CPSEs so that no further closure of the CPSEs takes place.  Since privately run 
enterprises/industries are thrivi ng, the Ministry should analyse the causes of its CPSEs' 
sickness and loss-making and make concerted efforts for their revival/restoration. 
(Para 65) 
 
25. The Committee having observed  that as on 31.01.2025, the actual utilization of 
funds by several Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) through Internal & Extra 
Budgetary Resources (IEBR) remains significantly low compared to the Annual Plan for 
2024-25. It recommends that the Ministry identif y the reasons for this under -utilization 
and take necessary measures to ensure that the funds raised are effectively utilized before 
the end of the current financial year. 
(Para 67) 
 
26.   The Committee noted that Rs. 500.00 crore has been allocated for the first time for 
the Payment Security Mechanism . The funds will be utilized by Convergence Energy 
Services Limited (CESL) to act as a payment security mechanism or a financial safeguard 
against the pa yments related to the 38,000 e -buses targeted unde r the scheme. It 
recommends that the Ministry ensure the efficient and timely utilization of these funds to 
support the successful implementation of the programme.  
(Para 70)

27. The Committee observed that no budgetary allocation has been made under the

the Ministry. Emphasizing the need for a skilled workforce in the evolving industrial 
landscape, it recommends that sufficient funds be sought at the RE stage (2025 -26) in 
collaboration with the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship to impart 
vocational training to local for enhancing their employability  and strengthen India's 
industrial competitiveness. 
(Para 71)

Discussion with Representatives of the Ministry of Heavy Industries 
The Chairman welcomed the Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) officials to discuss the 2025 -26 
Budget. He highlighted/ stated/ asked for 
(i) MHI's role is to develop capital goods, automobile, and heavy electrical equipment sectors 
while overseeing CPSEs and autonomous organisations.  
(ii) MHI's budget allocation for 2025-26 is about 85% of the proposed ₹9,025.83 crores. 
(iii) Action plan for optimally utilising the enhanced budgetary allocation for 2025-26, focusing 
on the PM E-Drive Scheme, which has been allocated more than 50% of the total budget.  
(iv) Information on schemes’ progress, strategies planned for the year, and the targets set.  
(v) Data on performance of CPSEs, steps taken to improve output and productivity, and any 
restructuring or revival plans for sick or loss-making CPSEs.  
2. After the Chair’s permission, through a presentation, the Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI)  
(i) outlined their budget performance from 2020-21 to 2024-25,  
(ii) focused on schemes like the PLI -Automobile Scheme, with an outlay of ₹25,938 crore, 
aimed at boosting the electric vehicle sector,  
(iii) Shared the technological advancements and significant growth of the Heavy Electrical 
Industry and 
(iv) Highlighted the importance of developing Advanced Chemistry Cells to accelerate the 
production of electric vehicles (EVs).  
(v) Provided an overview of the automotive industry, highlighting India’s global position in the 
sector, and discussed the awareness programs launched by the Ministry to educate the 
public about electric vehicles (EVs).  
(vi) Stressed the need to scale up manufacturing capabilities, create jobs, and improve India's 
position in the global automotive market.  
3. The CMDs briefed the Committee about BHEL, Bridge and Roof Company Ltd, and 
Braithwaite Burn and Joseph Construction Co. Ltd.  
4. After the presentation, the Chairman and Committee Members  
(i) Raised underutilisation of the budget in previous years, ranging from 2022-23 to 2024-25 
(ii) Pointed out the reduced allocation under capital heads vis a vis the total allocation; 
(iii) Sought reasons for continuing the legacy name of Braithwaite Burn and Jessop. 
(iv) Inquired about the steps taken to protect domestic players given global players like Tesla 
entering the Indian market 
(v) Sought replies on points like job work, underground coal gasification, coll aboration with 
J&T, Hyderabad for skill development, gravitational storage for large-scale solutions. 

40 
 
(vi) Highlighted that a key challenge is the customs duty on scrap material. When specialized 
material is imported for manufacturing, such as a one -tonne valve, the duty is charged on 
the full weight, including scrap, which adds unnecessary costs. The committee recommends 
addressing this issue with the Ministry of Finance or Commerce. Additionally, large 
companies like BHEL, with their technological capabilities, should focus more on job work 
opportunities. 
(vii) Reminded CMD HEC for the background note, as the Committee intends to recommend 
steps to revive the organisation 
5. The Committee directed that the following be recommended in their DFG report: 
(i) Passenger vehicles (four wheelers) and hybrid vehicles may also be incentivised under the 
PM E-Drive Scheme,  
(ii) Disbursement of incentives under PM E-Drive be streamlined and expedited,  
(iii) Additional funds be allocated to CPSEs, in collaboration with Ministry of Skill 
Development and Entrepreneurship to impart vocational training to locals for enhancing 
their employability 
(iv) Subsidies be offered for scrapping diesel vehicles when purchasing electric vehicles. 
6. The Chairman thanked the Secretary and other Officers for their input and requested that they 
provide written replies to the queries of Hon’ble MP to the Secretariat within 3 days.  
II Discussion with Representatives of Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises 
(MSME) 
7. The Chairman welcomed the Secretary  and Officers of the Ministry of MSME and its allied 
agencies to the meeting to discuss the Ministry’s budgetary allocations for FY 2025-26, and he 
(i) Acknowledged the increase in the MSME sector's budget allocation for 2025-26 to ₹23,168 
crore, up from ₹22,137.95 crore in the previous financial year,  
(ii) Inquired about the impact of less -allocation(by ₹2,439.08 crore) from the Ministry's 
projected ₹25,607.23 croreon the operation of various schemes, 
(iii) Expressed concern about the capital expenditure allocation, only 3% of the total budget, 
(iv) Sought the strategies for optimal budget utilisation, employment generation for micro and 
small enterprises, technological upgradation and enhanced R&D investment in the sector, 
(v) Asked for the reasons for rise in MSME closures, wit h 32,000 shutting down in FY 2024 -
25, compared to 175 in FY 2020-21  
(vi) Sought sector-wise breakdown of NPAs from RBI; 
(vii) Expressed concern on underutilisation of funds allocated to KVIC. 
8. After the Chair’s permission, the Secretary, M/o MSME apprised the Committee on the 
2025-26 budget highlights, including  
(i) Key measures to strengthen the sector, including increased investment and turnover limits, 
doubling of credit guarantee cover, a ₹5 la kh credit scheme for Udyam -registered micro-
enterprises, and a ₹10,000 crore Fund of Funds for startups. 
(ii) Focus and sectoral growth in footwear, leather, toys, and clean tech, with MSMEs 
contributing 30.1% of India’s GDP and ₹12.39 lakh crore in exports.  

41 
 
(iii) Continued support of artisans and MSMEs through schemes like PM Vishwakarma and 
PMEGP, with 25% of public procurement reserved for MSMEs. 
(iv) Reclassification of MSMEs and showcasing significant growth in the MSME sector, with 
registered MSMEs set to rise from 1.65 crore in 2023 to 6 crore by 2025 
(v) Increased (21X) procurement from SC -ST MSEs over the past decade under the National 
SC-ST Hub (NSSH).  
(vi) Emphasizing sustainable development, the Ministry aims to improve access to credit, 
market opportunities, technolog ical support, and infrastructure, ultimately driving the 
MSME sector’s growth as a key engine of the Indian economy, 
(vii) Introducing customised credit cards for micro-enterprises to address the credit gap. 
(viii) Lays a target of supporting 5.55 lakh MSMEs between 20 22 and 2027, with partnerships 
across 34 states.  
(ix) Significant increase in registered MSMEs, projected to reach 6 crore, with continued efforts 
to reduce credit gaps, enhance scalability, and drive investment.  
 
9. The Committee directed that the following be recommended in their DFG report: 
(i) The Government may revise the definition of Micro, Small, and Medium and if required, 
create a new category (nano or any other name) with lowest financial criteria (say, around 
Rs. 10 Lakh) arguing that businesses with a turnover above ₹2.5 crore might not align with 
the core purpose of MSMEs3 
(ii) RBI may regulate a uniform and streamlined interest/ margin rate for MSMEs across banks.

CHAPTER-1 
INTRODUCTION 
 
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises 
 
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) envisions a progressive 
MSME sector by promoting growth and development of small business, including khadi, village 
and coir industries, in cooperation with Ministries/Departments, State Governments and other 
stakeholders, by providing support to existing enterprises, adopting cutting edge technologies 
and encouraging creation of new enterprises. The Ministry is dedicated to fostering inclusive 
growth by ensuring geographic inclusivity of rural and urban areas, demographic inclusivity of 
socially and economically weaker sections such as Scheduled Castes (SCs) / Scheduled Tribes 
(STs)  communities, and promoting women entrepreneurship to boost gender parity. 
 
2. To promote and develop the MSME sector in the country, the Ministry is supported by 
various statutory and non-statutory bodies, including the Khadi and Village Industries 
Commission (KVIC), the Coir Board, National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC), National 
Institute for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (ni-MSME), and the Mahatma Gandhi 
Institute for Rural Industrialization (MGIRI). These organizations play a crucial role in fostering 
growth and providing support to the MSME sector 
 
3. The Ministry of MSME implements more than 25 schemes for credit support, 
technological assistance, infrastructure development, skill development, and training, enhancing 
competitiveness and market assistance to MSME, and creating self-employment opportunities. 
 
4. The Parliamentary Standing Committee, per its mandate, undertook a comprehensive 
assessment of the Ministry's detailed Demand for Grants. The Committee  
i. Reviewed various documents, including the Annual Report (2024-25), Economic Survey, 
Budget documents such as the Details of Demand for Grants, Output-Outcome 
Framework; 
ii. Examined the background note and the answers to the questionnaires; 
iii. Solicited evidence, interacted with and obtained replies from the Ministry. 
iv. Desktop research on Global Data related to MSMEs Sector. 
Public Procurement Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs ) 
5. The Ministry of MSME implemented the Public Procurement Policy for Micro and Small 
Enterprises (MSEs) under the MSMED Act, 2006, which became mandatory in 2015. The policy 
mandates that Public Sector companies procure 25% of their total purchases from MSEs, with 
4% reserved for SC/ST-owned MSEs and 3% for women-owned MSEs. The Ministry reduced 
the requirements from seven to four in August 2021 to ease compliance. 
6. Additionally, the MSME Sambandh Portal, launched in 2017, tracks procurement data, 
with 40.77% of total procurement reported from MSEs, benefiting over 161,000 MSEs. 
However, the participation of women and SC/ST-owned MSEs remains low at 2.32% and 
1.33%, respectively. The Ministry also encourages MSEs to join the Government e-Marketplace 
(GeM) Portal, with a simplified registration process integrated into the Udyam Registration 
online form. 

2 
 
7. While reviewing the performance of several CPSEs under the central Government, the 
National Hydro Power Corporation (NHPC) has displayed a strong example of successful policy 
implementation. It was observed that the NHPC has effectively engaged vendors, especially from 
remote areas by organizing vendor meetings at the project level to educate them on registration, 
obtaining Udyam certificates, and participating in the tendering process. Further, by uploading 
its annual procurement plan on a web portal, NHPC has ensured vendors have advance 
knowledge of requirements, thereby increasing eligible MSE participation in tenders. 
Recommendations 
8. The Committee, notes that despite efforts to implement sub-quotas within the Public 
Procurement Policy (PPP) for women and SC/ST-owned MSEs, significant gaps remain in 
achieving the quotas, with some regions reporting as low as 70% fulfillment. 
(i) In light of the success of the NHPC, the Committee recommends the MSME 
Ministry to take immediate and decisive action to eliminate barriers preventing the 
fulfillment of sub-quotas. The Ministry must prioritize the implementation of targeted 
measures to ensure full compliance and equitable distribution without delay.  
(ii) Additionally, it is suggested that the Ministry consider including Other Backward 
Classes (OBC)-owned MSEs within the overall PPP quotas, which could enhance their 
participation and further strengthen the policy's inclusivity and effectiveness. 
Budget Speech/Budget Highlights 
9. The Union Budget 2025-26 focuses on strengthening the MSME sector, recognizing it 
as second engine of India’s economic growth alongside agriculture, investment, and exports. 
With 6 crore registered MSMEs employing over 25 crore people and contributing 30% to the 
GDP, 36% to the manufacturing output, 45.73% to India’s total exports in 2023-24, and ₹5 lakh 
crore to GST, the sector plays a crucial role in manufacturing, exports, and employment. The 
new budget introduces a series of measures designed to foster innovation, improve 
competitiveness, and equip MSMEs to expand their reach and boost India’s economic 
development. Following are the highlights of the Union Budget 2025-26 for the MSME Sector:

Credit Cards for Micro Enterprises 
10. A new initiative will be introduced to empower micro enterprises registered on the 
Udyam portal by offering personalized credit cards with a ₹5 lakh limit. This initiative will 

3 
 
provide financial support to help these businesses grow, with 10 lakh cards set to be issued in the 
first year. 
Fund of Funds for Startups 
11. The Alternate Investment Funds (AIFs) for startups have secured commitments exceeding 
₹91,000 crore, supported by a Fund of Funds with a government contribution of ₹10,000 crore. A 
new Fund of Funds, with an expanded scope and an additional ₹10,000 crore contribution, will 
now be established to further support startups. 
Scheme for First-time Entrepreneurs  
12. A new scheme will be launched to support 5 lakh first-time women, Scheduled Castes, 
and Scheduled Tribes entrepreneurs by providing term loans of up to ₹2 crore over the next 5 
years. Drawing from the successful Stand-Up India scheme, it will also include online capacity 
building for entrepreneurship and managerial skills to empower these entrepreneurs. 
Focus Product Scheme for Footwear & Leather Sectors 
13. A focus product scheme will be implemented to enhance India's footwear and leather 
sectors’ productivity, quality, and competitiveness. The scheme will support design capacity, 
component manufacturing, and the necessary machinery for producing non-leather quality 
footwear, along with leather footwear and products. It is expected to generate employment for 22 
lakh people, achieve a turnover of ₹4 lakh crore, and drive exports exceeding ₹1.1 lakh crore..  
Measures for the Toy Sector 
14. Building on the National Action Plan for Toys, a new scheme will be implemented to 
make India a global toy hub. The scheme will focus on developing clusters, enhancing skills, and 
creating a robust manufacturing ecosystem. This will enable the production of high-quality, 
innovative, and sustainable toys that reflect the 'Made in India' brand, boosting India's presence in 
the global toy market. The global toy market is projected to experience significant growth in the 
coming years. Valued at approximately* ₹94,952 crore in 2024, the market is expected to 
generate revenues of around ₹1,10,273.8 crore in 2025. Looking further ahead, forecasts indicate 
the market will expand from US Dollar ₹1,00,015 crore to ₹1,68,573 crore by 2034, reflecting a 
compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 6%. This growth highlights the increasing demand and 
evolving trends within the global toy industry. 
Support for Food Processing 
15. In line with the commitment towards 'Purvodaya,' a National Institute of Food 
Technology, Entrepreneurship, and Management will be established in Bihar. This institute aims 
to boost food processing activities in the Eastern region, leading to enhanced income for farmers 
through value addition to their produce. It will also create skilling, entrepreneurship, and 
employment opportunities for the youth, fostering economic growth in the area. 
Manufacturing Mission - Furthering “Make in India” 
16. The Government will establish a National Manufacturing Mission to advance "Make in 
India" by offering policy support, execution roadmaps, and a governance and monitoring 
framework for both central ministries and states, covering small, medium, and large industries.

Export Promotion Mission  
17. An Export Promotion Mission will be established with sectoral and ministerial targets, 
led jointly by the Ministries of Commerce, MSME, and Finance. This mission will provide easy 
access to export credit, cross-border factoring support, and assist MSMEs in overcoming non-
tariff barriers in international markets. 
Global Scenario in MSMEs’ Classification 
18. The International Finance Corporation MSME definition* classifies enterprises as micro, 
small, or medium based on two of three criteria: employees, assets, or sales, or by the MSME 
loan size proxy. Micro enterprises have under 10 employees, assets, and sales below $100,000, 
with loans under $10,000, while small and medium enterprises have higher thresholds. 
Recommendations 
19. The Committee notes that, as of December 31, 2024, out of the 5.77 crore total 
MSMEs, 5.69 crore are micro, 7.3 lakh are small, and 69,000 are medium. Despite this, the 
new revised investment and turnover limits could potentially undermine the purpose of 
MSMEs by elevating micro-enterprises beyond their original scope. It is recommended that 
the Government revise the definition of Micro, Small, and Medium enterprises and create a 
new category –nano with the lowest financial criteria around ₹10 lakh. This would ensure 
that businesses with a turnover above ₹2.5 crore do not deviate from the core purpose of 
MSMEs—driving employment generation and supporting smaller enterprises. 
20. The Committee appreciates the new initiative to issue customized credit cards with a 
₹5 lakh limit for micro enterprises. It recommends that the Ministry expedite the 
distribution of these cards, focusing on micro enterprises that are not entirely digitised. 
Financial literacy programs should also be provided to help these businesses effectively 
utilize the cards, improving access to working capital and financial services.

Recommendations 
24. On Budget Utilization:-  
(i) The Committee recommends that the Ministry prioritize the optimal 
utilization of the allocated ₹23,168.15 crore by focusing on high-impact schemes, 
particularly those supporting technological upgradation, market access, and employment 
generation. To address the ₹2,439.08 crore shortfall, the Ministry may seek additional 
funds at the Revised Estimates (RE) stage or explore alternative funding sources, such as 
public-private partnerships (PPP) and collaborations with financial institutions, to ensure 
the uninterrupted implementation of critical programs. 
 (ii)  The Committee committee observes with concern that there is a significant 
gap between the Revised Estimate and actual expenditure, and a clear under achievement 
in the QEP, with only 41.74% of the allocated budget utilised as of January 20, 2025. This 
shortfall is attributed to challenges posed by the Model Code of Conduct during the general 
elections. The Committee recommends that the Ministry must adopt a more flexible and 
efficient planning approach to mitigate such disruptions in the future. Additionally, it 
should explore methods to accelerate fund utilization in the remaining months of the fiscal 
year to minimize any long-term impact on program outcomes. 
25. With regard to QEP targets set for the Financial Year 2025-26, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry apply lessons learned from the previous year by 
implementing a clear Quarterly and Monthly Expenditure Plan to ensure efficient fund 
utilization. Additionally, the Ministry should focus on strengthening initiative planning, 
execution, and budget absorption capacity to guarantee that allocated funds are utilized 
effectively, driving tangible outcomes in MSME initiatives. 
26. The Committee notes that 96.9% of the Ministry's budget allocation is allocated to 
revenue expenditure, with only 3.1% earmarked for capital expenditure. To drive 
substantial growth and achieve encouraging outcomes, the Ministry should prioritize 
increasing capital expenditure, as this will give an impetus to infrastructure and 
developmental initiatives. 
27. The Committee acknowledges that most schemes are demand-driven, but it 
recommends that the Ministry set clear, predefined targets for these schemes. IT 
recommends utilizing behavioural science tools to nudge, encourage, and motivate 
organisations, leading to better stakeholder outcomes. 
28. The Committee has observed the following in the explanatory note submitted by the 
Ministry on the proposed Revenue and Capial Outlays – 
i. High Savings in Non-Functional Heads: A large portion of savings was seen in non-
functional heads under the revenue section. Although funds were re-appropriated to 
functional heads for specific regions like the North East and Sikkim, the non-functional 
heads remained underutilized. 
ii. Delayed Scheme Approvals: Several schemes, including MSME Champions and MSME 
Innovative Scheme, were delayed in approval and launch, resulting in zero or minimal 
expenditure since funds couldn’t be utilized until later in the fiscal year. 

8 
 
iii. Lack of Proposals for Demand-Driven Schemes: Demand-driven schemes like Prime 
Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP) and Entrepreneur Skill 
Development Programme (ESDP) experienced savings due to the lack of viable 
proposals. Insufficient participation and low proposal submissions led to funds not being 
fully utilized. 
iv. Delayed Sanctioning Process for Infrastructure Development: Infrastructure 
development schemes saw savings due to delays in the sanctioning process and the low 
number of project proposals received, leading to underutilization of allocated funds. 
v. Zero Expenditure under PMEGP and other Credit Schemes & Self Reliant 
Initiative (SRI) Fund Schemes: The SRI Fund of Fund schemes had no expenditure, as 
the funds were dependent on daughter funds raising their own resources, which caused 
delays in deploying the allocated funds. 
vi. Underutilization of Infrastructure Establishment Funds: The infrastructure 
establishment fund also saw savings due to the non-receipt of viable project proposals, 
leading to unspent funds being surrendered. 
vii. High Percentage of Unutilized Funds: Many schemes, such as the Infrastructure 
Development Programme and Research and Evaluation Studies, saw high savings, mainly 
due to delayed approvals and insufficient demand for the schemes. 
And based on these observations the Committee recommends that  
29. The Ministry should establish a structured timeline for the approval and launch of 
schemes to ensure timely operationalization and prevent delays, as seen with the MSME 
Champions and MSME Innovative Schemes. Allocating funds to functional heads at the 
start of the fiscal year will reduce re-appropriations and streamline project 
implementation. To tackle underutilization due to insufficient proposals, the Ministry 
should enhance efforts to engage potential proposers, especially for demand-driven 
schemes like PMEGP, ESDP, and the Infrastructure Development Programme, through 
more targeted awareness campaigns, workshops, webinars, and networking events. A 
robust monitoring system may also be implemented to track proposal submissions, 
ensuring timely follow-ups and support. 
 
30.  The Ministry should prioritize the prompt deployment of capital funds, particularly 
for the SRI Fund of Fund & PMEGP and other credit schemes by collaborating with 
daughter funds to mobilize resources quickly and establishing follow-up mechanisms for 
fund deployment. To improve utilization of infrastructure-related funds, the sanctioning 
process may be expedited, and project proposals should be regularly solicited. An effective 
real-time monitoring system should track fund utilization, enabling quick identification of 
underutilization and corrective actions. Periodic reviews of fund allocation will ensure 
alignment with actual needs. Ministry may focus more towards strengthening coordination 
with implementing agencies and introducing flexibility in fund reallocation will help 
optimize resource usage, reduce savings, and address delays. Additionally, enhancing the

MAJOR SCHEMES AND PROGRAMMES 
33. The Ministry of MSME has introduced various dynamic and comprehensive schemes to 
promote the growth and development of Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises across India. 
These initiatives focus on key areas such as finance, technology, infrastructure, employment 
generation, entrepreneurship, and marketing. Most of these schemes are managed under three 
divisions of the ministry: the Small and Medium Enterprises (SME) Division, the Agro and 
Rural Industry (ARI) Division, along with the Office of the Development Commissioner (DC, 
MSME), an attached office. The major schemes covering 80% of their budgetary allocation of 
the Ministry and their budget analysis are as below:- 
GUARANTEED EMERGENCY CREDIT LINE (GECL) 
34. The Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS), launched on 23rd May 2020 as 
part of the Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyaan, aimed to support MSMEs and other businesses 
impacted by the COVID-19 crisis. The scheme provided a 100% guarantee to Member Lending 
Institutions (MLIs) on credit extended to eligible borrowers, enabling businesses to meet 
operational liabilities and resume activities. Implemented by the Department of Financial 
Services (DFS) under the Ministry of Finance, the scheme was operational until 31st March 
2023. According to a research report by SBI dated 23rd January 2023, the scheme protected 
nearly 14.6 lakh MSME accounts, with 98.3% of these being from the micro and small enterprise 
categories, and helped prevent about 12% of outstanding MSME credit from being classified as 
non-performing assets (NPAs). 
35. The allocation for the ECLGS is determined based on the demand raised by the DFS and 
the National Credit Guarantee Trustee Company (NCGTC). While the scheme was designed to 
act as a safeguard fund in case of NPAs arising from loans extended during the pandemic, there 
has been no shortage of funds for credit guarantee coverage. In fact, Rs. 5 lakh crore worth of 
credit guarantees have been provided over the last two years. As NPAs within MSMEs have 
been declining, the budgetary allocations for the GECL scheme are no longer required to be fully 
utilized. Similarly, for other smaller schemes, the allocations have either remained consistent or 
increased, demonstrating the continued need for support without concerns of unutilized funds.

CREDIT SUPPORT/GUARANTEE SCHEMES 
37. The Credit Guarantee Scheme for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE) offers 
collateral-free credit to MSEs through banks, financial institutions, and NBFCs. The scheme's 
loan ceiling was increased from ₹2 crore to ₹5 crore per borrowing unit as of April 1, 2023, with 
up to 90% guarantee coverage. The scheme supports women-led enterprises with enhanced 
coverage and charges a nominal Annual Guarantee Fee (AGF). As of December 2024, the 
scheme has approved 1.01 crore proposals totalling ₹8.07 lakh crore, benefiting MSEs across 
more than 100 sectors, with a significant focus on underserved regions. 
38. In FY 2023-24, the government infused ₹9,000 crore into the CGTMSE corpus, which 
includes ₹8,500 crore from GoI and ₹500 crore from SIDBI (Small Industries Development 
Bank of India). Revamped measures, such as a 50% reduction in guarantee fees and simplified 
claims processing for loans up to ₹10 lakh, are designed to reduce credit costs for MSEs and 
enhance their growth potential. These changes aim to boost credit access and foster the 
development of small businesses, particularly in rural and regional areas. 
39. CGTMSE has leveraged digital platforms to streamline the application process for 
guarantee coverage, with automated approvals and API integration with 13 major banks for 
seamless data flow. These digital advancements led to a significant rise in guarantee approvals, 
reaching ₹2.04 lakh crore by January 31, 2025, surpassing the previous year's record of ₹2.02 
lakh crore. In the upcoming financial year, CGTMSE plans further digital enhancements, 
including complete end-to-end API (Application Programming Interface) integration with MLIs 
(Member Lending Institutions) and improvements to user interfaces and experiences.

RAISING AND ACCELERATING MSME PERFORMANCE (RAMP) 
58. The RAMP (Raising and Accelerating MSME Performance) scheme is a World Bank-
assisted Central Sector initiative to boost MSME performance by promoting innovation, 
digitisation, technology upgradation, market access, credit, and sustainability initiatives. With a 
total outlay of ₹6062.45 crore from FY 2022-23 to FY 2026-27, the World Bank provides ₹3750 
crore (USD 500 million) in support. 
59. Besides providing gap funding to States under Strategic Investment Plans (SIPs), RAMP 
supports various MSME schemes, including the MSME Champions Scheme, Procurement and 
Marketing Support, and International Cooperation. It also introduces four new sub-schemes: the 
MSE Green Investment and Financing for Transformation (MSE GIFT Scheme), MSE Scheme 
for Circular Economy Promotion (MSE SPICE Scheme), MSE Online Dispute Resolution 
(ODR) for Delayed Payments, and MSME Trade Enablement & Marketing (MSME TEAM) 
Initiative. The programme is expected to benefit over 5.5 lakh MSMEs during its five-year 
duration. 
60. Besides, it is informed that all 36 States and Union Territories (UTs) are participating in 
the RAMP Scheme, with each receiving a grant of ₹5 crore to prepare a Strategic Investment 
Plan (SIP) for the development and promotion of the MSME sector. 34 States/UTs have 
submitted SIPs, and a total of ₹2966.144 crore has been approved for selected projects within 
these plans. The first instalment of grants has been released to these States/UTs to implement the 
approved projects.
